Vegetation management The single most overlooked prevention strategy. **Tree branches** touching the roofline are rodent highways — trim to at least 3 feet of clearance, and 6 is better. Keep **shrubs and plantings** 12 to 18 inches off the foundation. Replace dense **ground cover** within 12 inches of the foundation with gravel or bare soil. Store **firewood** at least 20 feet from the home, off

Gutters and drainage In our rainy climate, gutter management isn't optional. Clean gutters at least twice a year, and more often in heavily treed areas. Ensure downspouts discharge 4 to 6 feet from the foundation, and grade soil to slope away from the house at least 6 inches over the first 10 feet. Clogged gutters overflow against the foundation and hold standing water, which is exactly the condit

sections: What does Integrated Pest Management actually mean? At its core, IPM is a decision-making framework. Rather than treating pest control as a single action — spray the house, repeat next month — it treats it as a system with multiple layers, each chosen to address the specific situation. The **integrated** part means combining several complementary strategies instead of relying on any one, and alway

How is IPM different from traditional pest control? Traditional pest control has often meant a reactive, chemical-first routine: a pest appears, so you spray, and you keep spraying on a schedule whether or not it's needed. Much of what drives pests here — rodents seeking warmth, ants following moisture, dampwood termites and other pests drawn to wet wood — comes back to moisture and access, exactly the kind of root causes IPM targets. title: What Is Rodent Exclusion, and Why Traps Alone Fail
sections: What is rodent exclusion, exactly? Rodent exclusion is a two-part process. First, a systematic look over the entire structure to identify every point where rodents are entering or could enter. Second, the physical sealing of those openings with materials that rodents cannot gnaw, squeeze, or force their way through.

Why won't traps alone solve a rodent problem in Bellingham? Traps remove individual rodents, but they do nothing to close the door that let those rodents in. Bellingham and Whatcom County have large, established populations of roof rats, Norway rats, and house mice. These animals are territorial: when one is removed, neighboring individuals move into the vacated territory quickly.

How is rodent exclusion different from pest control? Traditional pest control, whether trapping or rodenticide, is **reactive**. It responds to an existing problem. Rodent exclusion is **proactive and structural**. It modifies the building itself to make rodent entry far harder.
What does a rodent exclusion visit cover? A professional look over a Whatcom County home is far more thorough than most homeowners expect. Here is what we go over:
What materials are used in rodent exclusion? Effective exclusion requires materials that are impervious to rodent gnawing, which rules out wood, standard caulk, and expanding foam on their own.

How long does rodent exclusion last? Done correctly with the right materials, most exclusion repairs are long-lasting. Hardware cloth, steel flashing, and mortar repairs do not degrade meaningfully over a normal home's lifespan.

Is rodent exclusion worth the investment? In almost every case, yes. The damage a rodent infestation causes quickly outpaces the cost of prevention. Rodents chew electrical wiring, which is a fire hazard, and contaminate insulation with urine and droppings so that it then needs replacing. They damage structural wood, HVAC ducts, and stored belongings. Replacing attic insulation alone, after a seri

Can you do rodent exclusion yourself? Some basic steps are reasonable DIY projects: replacing a worn door sweep, caulking a low-risk cable entry point, or installing a cover over a crawl space vent. The challenge with comprehensive DIY exclusion is thoroughness. Most homeowners seal the obvious gaps but miss several less obvious ones, and a rodent only needs one. title: Wood-Boring Beetle Treatment After a Flood
sections: Flooding creates the conditions wood-destroying insects need Wood-boring beetles favor moist, untreated wood. After flooding, framing members, subfloors, sill plates, and joists often hold elevated moisture long after the surfaces feel dry. That damp environment is exactly what these beetles need in order to lay eggs in the wood, and for the larvae to develop inside it.
Why treatment should happen *before* insulation installation Installing new insulation without addressing wood-destroying insects means covering up a problem you can no longer see.

Drying comes first Treatment is not a substitute for drying the structure out. Wood-boring beetles and wood decay fungi are both moisture problems at heart, and neither is solved while the wood stays wet. Decay fungi in particular need wood well above the roughly 20 percent moisture content generally considered safe — serious decay takes hold as wood approaches the fiber saturation point near 30 p

Protect your home before moving forward At **Sasquatch Pest Control**, we see elevated wood-destroying insect risk in homes following a flood. Treating now — **before insulation and repairs are completed** — is the practical move for homeowners, builders, and restoration contractors alike.

title: Yellow Jackets in Whatcom County: What to Know
sections: What Are Yellow Jackets? Yellow jackets are social wasps that live in large colonies, sometimes consisting of thousands of members. Unlike honeybees, which die after stinging once, yellow jackets have smooth stingers and can attack multiple times. They are particularly aggressive in late summer when their colonies reach peak numbers and food sources become scarce.
Where Do Yellow Jackets Nest? Yellow jackets construct their nests using chewed wood fibers mixed with saliva, creating a paper-like structure. These nests can be found:

Why Are Yellow Jackets Dangerous? Unlike honeybees, which pollinate flowers and produce honey, yellow jackets are carnivorous predators that feed on other insects, meats, and sugary foods. Their aggressive nature and ability to sting multiple times make them particularly hazardous. For those allergic to their venom, a single sting can trigger severe reactions, including anaphylaxis.

Yellow Jacket Control with Sasquatch Pest Control The best time to deal with yellow jackets is early, while the colony is still small. Sasquatch Pest Control treats nests at the source and works on the conditions that make a property attractive to them in the first place.

Don't Wait Until It's Too Late If you've noticed an increase in yellow jacket activity around your property, now is the time to act. Getting to a nest early is far easier and far safer than dealing with a mature colony in August, and our team is here to help your home stay a good deal more comfortable through the rest of the season.

Where we work Multifamily and property management work is concentrated in **Bellingham** —
Sehome, Happy Valley, the Lettered Streets, City Center, Cordata and Barkley —
and runs out through **Ferndale**, **Lynden**, **Blaine** and **Birch Bay**, and
south into **Mount Vernon**, **Burlington** and **Sedro-Woolley**. Single
buildings, portfolios and HOA-managed communities are all the same category

Starting We walk the building, not a unit. That walk covers the crawlspace and attic
where they are shared, the common areas, waste handling, the exterior envelope,
and enough units to understand the construction rather than to inventory the
complaints.

title: Restaurant Pest Control | Bellingham & Whatcom
sections:
Judged on an ordinary Tuesday A processing plant is audited on its records over a year. A restaurant is judged
on a walkthrough that arrives without an appointment, looks at what is there
that day, and writes down what it sees. The rules behind that walkthrough trace
back to the [FDA Food Code](https://www.fda.gov/food/retail-food-protection/fda-food-code),
the model state and local regulators bui

The three that account for most of it **Drains and the organic film.** The single largest source of recurring
complaints in food service, and the one most often treated at the wrong end.
Small flies — drain flies, phorid flies, fruit flies — do not fly in. They breed
in a film of organic material, and a restaurant produces that film continuously
in drain lines, under equipment plinths, in floor cr

Cockroaches, and the difference between elimination and management German cockroaches are the defining restaurant pest, and it is worth being clear
about something the trade is often vague on: a German cockroach population can
be eliminated. Not suppressed, not managed — eliminated. If a program is not
aiming at that, you are buying maintenance on a problem that did not have to be
permanent.

Rodents in a restaurant Inside Bellingham the rodent picture is rats — Norway rats at ground level using
foundations, drains and voids, and roof rats where trees, wires or a fence reach
a roofline. Mice are more of a county animal than a city one, which surprises
people.

Bars, breweries and taprooms Bellingham has an unusual density of breweries and taprooms for a city this
size, and they are not simply restaurants that serve less food. The pest picture
is different enough to be worth its own paragraph.

Patios, decks and outdoor service Outdoor seating extended the season here and it added exposure, so it is worth
saying what changes.

Shared buildings, which change the scope A great deal of Bellingham's food service sits in connected buildings: downtown
blocks, Fairhaven, strip retail on the arterials, and converted older stock
where a restaurant shares a wall, a chase and a roof void with a neighbor.

Working around service Discretion and scheduling are not a nicety in food service, they are most of
what makes a program tolerable.

Grease, waste and the outside of the building The exterior is where most restaurant pest pressure is generated, and it is
usually somebody else's job, which is why it drifts.

The record, and what to have ready Restaurants do not face the annual audit burden a processing plant does, but
there is a version of it and it turns up unannounced.

Staff, and the part training actually changes Every restaurant has turnover, and pest outcomes track a small number of
behaviors that new staff do not automatically know:

The year in food service **Spring.** Small fly pressure begins as temperatures rise. Ants appear,
predominantly odorous house ants, and a repellent spray from a cash-and-carry
will split the colony rather than kill it.

Where we work Restaurant and food service work runs across **Bellingham** — downtown,
Fairhaven, the Guide Meridian and Sunset corridors, and the neighborhood
kitchens between them — and out through **Ferndale**, **Lynden**, **Blaine**,
**Birch Bay** and **Sudden Valley**, then south into **Mount Vernon**,
**Burlington** and **Sedro-Woolley**. Cafes, bars, breweries, taprooms, bakeries,
commissari

Starting We walk the site with somebody who knows the kitchen, ideally outside service.
The walk covers receiving, dry storage, the line, the dish area, drains and the
mop sink, the walk-in surrounds, ceiling voids where they are accessible, the
back door, and the dumpster enclosure — which is usually the most informative
five minutes of the visit.

title: Retail & Grocery Pest Control | Whatcom County
sections:
Most of it arrives in a box The defining fact about retail pest control is that the building is usually not
where the problem starts. The delivery is.

The back room decides it The sales floor gets all the attention and almost none of the pest activity. The
work is behind the door marked staff only.

Grocery and food retail Food retail adds the whole of food service's problems and a great deal more
surface area.

Convenience stores and gas stations A c-store is a small building with a disproportionate pest load, and it is worth
separating because the shape of the problem is different.

Shared buildings and strip retail A great deal of retail in this county is in connected buildings: strip centers
on the arterials, downtown blocks in Bellingham and Fairhaven, and the retail
corridor through Burlington.

Rodents in retail Inside Bellingham the picture is rats — Norway rats at ground level working
foundations, drains and voids, roof rats where the roofline, a fence line or
trees give access. Sites out toward the county see more mice off surrounding
open ground.

Small flies and where they breed Retail small fly complaints are almost always one of four things, and none of
them is solved by treating the air:

Stored product insects, which are a stock problem Worth separating out, because the instinct on a beetle or a moth sighting is to
treat the room and the room is almost never the source.

Birds at the entrance Droppings on an entrance canopy are a slip hazard where customers walk, and over
a dock they are a finding on any site handling food. Bird exclusion is not work
we do, so if that is the problem we will tell you plainly and recommend a
specialist.

Working around trading Almost all of this is done outside trading hours, and most of it is in areas
customers never enter anyway.

Garden centers and nurseries Worth a separate note, because they sit under retail and behave like nothing
else in it.

The record Food retail is inspected, and grocery in particular sits inside audit schemes
that ask for the pest program directly.

The year in retail **Late winter to spring.** Structural work at the dock and the service
penetrations, while the building is quiet and the weather allows exterior work.

What we ask of the store - A receiving standard, applied by somebody who actually looks, with a stated
  rejection point
- Cardboard broken down and baled or removed rather than stacked
- Stock rotation enforced, and splits dealt with the day they happen
- Racking kept clear of the floor and pallets moved periodically so the floor
  can be seen
- Waste on a schedule that holds in August, with encl

Where we work Retail and grocery work runs across **Bellingham** — downtown, Fairhaven, the
Guide Meridian and Sunset corridors, and the neighborhood centers — and out
through **Ferndale**, **Lynden**, **Blaine**, **Birch Bay** and **Sumas**, then
south into the **Burlington** retail corridor, **Mount Vernon** and
**Sedro-Woolley**. Grocery, convenience, pet supply, garden centers, pharmacy
and ge

Starting We walk the store outside trading hours with somebody who knows the back room.
The walk covers receiving and the dock, the stockroom and racking, cardboard
handling, the break room, waste and the enclosure, chillers and their
condensate, deli and bakery where they exist, floor voids and fixed equipment,
and the exterior.

title: School & Childcare Pest Control | Whatcom County
sections:
The statute shapes the program Most commercial pest work is shaped by the building. School work is shaped by
the law first and the building second, and that is not a complaint — it produces
better pest control than the alternative.

What a school building actually is A school is several different buildings pretending to be one, and the pest
picture changes between them.
The rodent picture on a campus Whatcom County schools sit in two different situations and it changes the work.

Cafeterias, and receiving The kitchen is the highest-consequence part of a school and it is run harder
than most commercial kitchens, so it deserves specific attention.

Ants, which are the most common classroom call By volume the thing a school actually rings about is ants in a classroom, and it
is worth setting out because the instinct is to treat it and the instinct is
wrong.

Older buildings, moisture and crawlspaces A good share of the school stock in this county is old enough to have the
problems old buildings have here, and moisture is the one that drives pest
pressure.
Fields, grounds and the outdoor edge The grounds are half a campus and they generate their own work.

What integrated pest management actually means here The phrase appears in every school pest contract in the country and it is worth
saying what it means in practice rather than as a slogan, because a district is
entitled to check whether it is getting it.

Bed bugs, and the reason to be careful Bed bugs are the school problem most likely to become a public one, and the
handling matters more than the treatment.

Licensed childcare, which is not a small school Childcare and preschool settings sit under the same notification requirements
and they are not simply schools at a smaller scale. Three things differ enough
to change the program.

Wasps, and the grounds Stinging insects are the school pest with the clearest safety edge, and the
season is unhelpfully timed: our heaviest weeks are August and September, which
is exactly when campuses reopen.

Working around the school year **Summer break.** The working window, and the reason a school program is planned
a year ahead. Buildings are empty, structural work is possible, portables can be
skirted properly, kitchens are down, and anything requiring notification can be
done without competing with the school day.

The record Schools keep records because the statute says so, and a district with several
sites needs those records organized by building rather than pooled.

What we ask of the district - A named contact per site, and one at district level who sees the roll-up
- Access to mechanical, custodial and kitchen spaces on visit days
- Receiving standards applied at every site rather than the best one
- Portable skirting treated as a maintained asset rather than as trim
- Waste enclosures that close, on a collection schedule that holds in June
- A route for st

Where we work School and childcare work runs across the districts in **Bellingham**,
**Ferndale**, **Lynden**, **Blaine**, **Meridian**, **Nooksack Valley** and
**Mount Baker**, and south into **Burlington**, **Sedro-Woolley** and **Mount
Vernon**. Licensed childcare, preschools and private schools are the same
category of work at a different scale, and the notification requirements reach
licensed

Starting We walk the estate, or a representative sample of it for a district, with
facilities and with nutrition services. The walk covers kitchens and receiving,
dry storage, custodial and mechanical spaces, portables and their skirting,
locker rooms, the ceiling and service voids where accessible, waste, and the
grounds.

title: Choosing a Pest Control Company in Whatcom County
sections:
What a useful version of this page looks like Most articles on choosing a pest control company are written by pest control
companies and list criteria the writer happens to meet. That is an advertisement
with a numbered list in it.

Start with the license, because it is free and public Washington licenses this trade, and the licenses are a matter of public record.
The Washington State Department of Agriculture runs a license search on its own
site, open to anybody, at no cost. There is no reason to take a company's word
for its licensing when the state will tell you directly.
The credential most people do not know exists Here is the part that decides whether this page is honest.

The questions that actually separate good from bad Long question lists are easy to produce and hard to use. These five do most of
the work.

Red flags, in rough order of how much they should worry you **A quote without a visit.** For anything beyond a wasp nest you can point at,
this is not a price. The two variables that move a job most in this county —
what the crawlspace is like, and how open the building is — cannot be judged
from a phone call. A figure given before either is known will move once someone
arrives.

What a license does not tell you Worth saying, because the licensing section above could give the wrong
impression. A license is a floor, not a recommendation.

On price, briefly Price is the thing people want to lead with and the thing that tells you least
early on, because two quotes for the same problem are usually two different
jobs. What is included, whether repair work is in or out, how many visits, and
what the terms are on coming back all move the figure more than any margin does.
Franchise or local, which is the wrong question People ask this a lot and it is not the axis that decides anything.

Insurance and the practical questions Ask whether the company carries general liability insurance and whether it can
produce a certificate. Most can, most will, and property managers and commercial
accounts should ask as a matter of routine rather than as a challenge.
What you are entitled to afterward Washington is specific about this and most customers do not know it.

Reviews, and what they can and cannot tell you Read the text, not the score. Almost every company in this trade shows a high
average, so the number carries very little signal. What carries signal is the
content: did the problem actually resolve, did the company come back when asked,
how do they respond when somebody is unhappy, and are the detailed reviews
describing the same service you are being

Where we are the wrong choice This is the section that makes the rest of the page worth reading, so it is
specific rather than modest.

If something goes wrong Most disagreements in this trade are about expectations rather than
competence, and most of them resolve in one phone call if the call happens
early. Say what you expected, say what happened, and ask what they propose. Do
it in writing as well as by phone, dated, and keep the copy.
Buying this for a business Briefly, because a commercial buyer is asking a different set of questions.
A short checklist Take this to whichever company you call, including this one.

title: Low-Impact Treatment: What It Can and Cannot Do
sections:
A phrase with nothing behind it There is no legal definition of eco-friendly pest control. No agency issues that
designation, no standard governs who may use the phrase, and no penalty attaches
to using it about a service that is identical to the one next door.

What the labeling rules actually permit Start with what a manufacturer is allowed to print, because it is stricter than
what a service company is allowed to say.
What genuinely lowers exposure Four things, in order of how much difference they make.
What is overstated Now the other half, and this is where the trade earns its reputation.

What we actually use, said plainly We use conventional registered products where they are the right tool for the
job, and we are not going to pretend otherwise to sound better.

Where the product actually ends up The exposure conversation usually happens at the level of the bottle. It is more
useful at the level of the surface.

Non-chemical tools that do real work Worth naming, because they get treated as marginal when several of them are the
main event.
Home remedies, briefly People ask, so it is worth answering rather than being smug about it.
The practical questions, if you have children, pets or a garden Ask these and you will learn more than any label on a van will tell you.

Pollinators, and being careful about what we claim Flowering plants in bloom are where bees are, and applications to blooming
vegetation are the ones with the clearest potential to reach them. Timing,
placement and simply not treating flowering material are the tools, and they
cost nothing.

Where a low-impact approach runs out of road Being honest about the limits is the other half of being honest about the
benefits.

The trade-off nobody states Lower impact usually means more work, and most of the extra work lands on the
occupant rather than the technician.

The summary a brochure will not print Most of what genuinely reduces exposure is not a product and is not sold by the
gallon. It is identification, restraint, closing the building, drying it out,
and putting a very small amount of the right material exactly where the insect
goes rather than a large amount where people walk.

title: Pest Control in Washington Schools
sections:
Why this page exists Schools ask us a version of the same question every year, usually in August:
what are we actually required to do before anybody sprays anything.

Who it applies to **RCW 17.21.415** sits within the Washington Pesticide Application Act and
covers public K-12 schools and licensed day care facilities.

The 48-hour rule The core requirement: notify interested parents or guardians of students, and
employees, **at least forty-eight hours before** a pesticide application.
What the notification must contain The statute is specific. A notification must state:
Signs Two sizes, depending on where.

Records Records of applications must be kept and an **annual summary** made readily
accessible to interested persons.
The exemptions, and the one that matters Four exemptions:

What an IPM program in a school actually looks like Integrated pest management is a term that gets used loosely, so here is what it
means in a school building in practical terms.

The pests schools in this county actually get Generic school pest advice tends to be written around cockroaches in warm
climates. Whatcom County buildings produce a different list, and the differences
change what a sensible program looks like.

Building the year around the calendar Since the pressure is seasonal and a school year has natural gaps in it, the
scheduling almost writes itself — and the gaps line up with an exemption.
The structural items are the real work A pattern we see in institutional buildings, and schools in particular.

Private schools, higher education and other facilities The statute names public K-12 schools and licensed day care facilities. That
leaves several kinds of institution asking whether it applies to them, and the
honest answer is that it depends on what you are.

Liability, briefly The section of the statute that sets all this out is titled, in part,
"liability" — and the notification and record-keeping requirements are the
mechanism by which a school demonstrates it did what was required.

Questions worth asking a contractor If you are procuring pest control for a school or a licensed facility, these
separate the serious from the rest.

One thing worth doing this month Whatever month you are reading this in, there is a version of the next useful
step.

What we do We work schools and institutional buildings the same way we work everything
else, which is exclusion-first, with treatment where it is warranted and not
where it is not.

title: Sealing a Building Before Fall
sections:
The six weeks that decide the winter There is a specific, narrow, and slightly unfair fact underneath almost every
winter pest call in Whatcom County: the problem arrived during a six-week
stretch in the autumn, through openings that were there all year, and the only
cheap moment to have done something about it was several weeks before anybody
had a reason to think about it.

What is actually arriving, and why it all arrives together Two entirely separate groups move toward buildings on the same schedule, for the
same reason, through the same gaps. That coincidence is what makes late-summer
sealing such good value, because one afternoon's work addresses both.

Why the wall void changes everything The reason the calendar is so unforgiving is that the barrier between "outside"
and "inside a cavity" is the only barrier that matters, and it is one-way in
practice.

Walking the building Allow an hour. Go in order rather than wandering, take notes, and photograph
anything you are not going to fix today. This is roughly the order we work in.

Materials, which is where most of this fails Correct material fastened badly is a flap, not a barrier. Wrong material
fastened well is worse, because it looks finished.

Screening is not blocking One error is common enough to warrant its own warning, and it is usually made by
somebody being conscientious.
What to do yourself, and what to hand over There is a real division here and it is mostly about height and confined space.
Sequence, which matters more than thoroughness Three steps, in this order, always.
The honest position on the timing This page argues against our own autumn.
If it is already autumn The advice does not become useless, it just changes shape.

Related work The service page for this is
[pest exclusion and repairs](/services/exclusion-and-repairs/), which covers
materials, the crawlspace and what we will and will not take on. The specific
jobs most of this walk produces are
[sealing a quarter-inch foundation gap](/services/exclusion-and-repairs/sealing-a-quarter-inch-foundation-gap/)
and
[crawlspace vent screening](/services/exclusion-and

title: The Commercial Pest Year in Whatcom County
sections:
What is different about a commercial year The organisms are the same ones a house gets. The calendar is the same calendar.
What differs is the building and what happens when something is seen.

The documentation question, taken first Everything else on this page is easier to plan once this part is settled, so it
goes at the front.
January and February **Quiet outside, busy inside, and the best two months for administration.**
March and April **The ground warms and the outdoor pressure resumes.**
May and June **The dry ground months, and the only practical window for groundwork.**

July and August **The most important eight weeks in the commercial year, and the ones when
nothing appears to be wrong.**
September **Everything arrives at once, and the audit calendar tends to arrive with it.**
October and November **The peak of the indoor year, and the point at which prevention has closed.**
December **Settled in, and quiet in a misleading way.**

Deliveries, the route that ignores the calendar Everything above is weather-driven. One major route into a commercial building
is not, and it deserves its own heading because facilities consistently
underrate it.

The same year, by facility type The calendar above is the shape. Which parts of it hurt depends on what the
building does.
The structural items nobody owns A pattern worth naming, because it is where most commercial pest budgets leak.
The planning calendar, compressed If a facility manager takes one thing from this page, take the sequence.

How we work commercial accounts Exclusion first, monitoring second, treatment where it is warranted and not
where it is not. Practically: a walk of the envelope, the waste area and
receiving before anything is proposed; a program built on monitoring and
contained placements rather than scheduled broadcast application; structural
items written up every visit for facilities to action; records kept,

title: The Whatcom County Pest Year
sections:
Pest problems here run on a calendar Almost nothing that happens in a Whatcom County building is a surprise. The
insects and animals that turn up follow the weather, the weather here is
consistent enough to plan around, and the same calls arrive in the same weeks
every year.
January and February **Quiet for arrivals, busy for discoveries.**
March and April **The ground warms and things start moving.**
May and June **Growth, and the best month nobody uses.**
July and August **The peak of everything outdoors, and the window that matters.**
September **The month everything arrives at once.**
October and November **The peak of the indoor year.**
December **Rodents settled in, everything else dormant.**

The same year, by pest The month-by-month view above is how the year feels from inside a building.
Here is the same information organized by organism, which is more useful if you
already know what you are dealing with.
If you only do one walk a year Make it late July or early August, allow an hour, and look at these in order.
The pattern underneath Three things drive nearly all of that.
What the preceding season predicts Year-to-year variation is real and it is mostly set before you notice it.

Why the calendar differs across the county Whatcom County is not one place, and the same month lands differently depending
on where a building sits. The differences are consistent enough to plan around.

The version of this you can act on If you take one thing from the calendar, take this: **there are two months that
decide the year, and neither of them is the month you will feel like calling.**

What we will do Come out in the quiet months and walk the building with you — the crawlspace,
the foundation line, the roofline, the grounds — and leave you with a list in
priority order, with the items that are ours separated from the items that
belong to a drainage contractor, a roofer or an afternoon of your own.

title: WDO Reports in a Washington Property Sale
sections:
The confusion that costs two weeks Here is the sequence we see, several times a year, and it wastes the same
two weeks every time.

What counts as a wood-destroying organism Broader than people assume. In Washington the group covers organisms that
attack structural material: **fungus, termites, carpenter ants and wood-boring
beetles.**
Two different documents This is the part worth understanding properly.

Where we sit, precisely We want to be exact about this, because being vague about it would win us work
we should not have.

What actually has to happen after a finding A report with findings on it usually generates three separate pieces of work,
and confusing them is where money gets wasted.
Sequencing it so it does not take a month The order that saves time and money.

What we find behind these reports, in this county Since the point of a report is to tell you what is there, it is worth setting
out what "there" usually turns out to be in Whatcom County, because it differs
from the national picture in ways that matter to a transaction.

Reading a report without panicking Reports are written to be complete rather than to be reassuring, and a first
read tends to land badly. A few things that help.
The timeline, realistically Transactions run on dates, so here is what the treatment side actually takes.
For sellers Two things, both unglamorous.

For buyers **Read the excluded areas.** A complete report lists what could not be
inspected, and that list is genuinely informative. An inaccessible crawlspace
corner or a sealed area is not a clean bill of health for that area — it is a
gap in the picture, and it is disclosed precisely so you can weigh it.

An open question we are not resolving here In the interest of not overstating the position set out above: the WSDA
category description for PCO Structural indicates that the category may perform
*specific* wood destroying organism inspections — the proposal-and-estimate kind that
cannot be used in a transaction. WSPMA's material describes the same
distinction.

A note on refinancing Most of this page is written around a sale, because that is where the volume
is, but refinancing produces the same requirement and a slightly different
dynamic.

What we will do Come out, look at what has been found, and quote the treatment — free, and
usually within a couple of days.

title: What Drives the Cost of Pest Control
sections:
Why there is no price list here Somebody arrives at a page like this wanting a number, and the honest thing to
say first is that the number does not exist yet. Not because it is being
withheld, but because it has not been determined — the property determines it,
and nobody has looked at the property.
The pest, and whether the job has a shape or a cycle The first fork is not severity. It is biology.
Size, and then construction, which matters more Square footage is the obvious variable and the least interesting one.
Access, which is the biggest single swing in this county If one paragraph on this page saves you from a surprise, it is this one.

Severity, and how long it has been running These two get collapsed into one word — "bad" — and they are not the same
variable.

Treatment, repair, and the line between them This is the distinction that explains most of the confusion about pest control
pricing, and almost nobody sets it out.

One-off against recurring, argued both ways Recurring plans have a bad reputation, partly earned. Here is the case for each,
stated fairly.

The visit quote and the phone quote UC IPM's advice on hiring is direct: a company should identify the pest, show
you the problem areas, and give you a written diagnosis and a plan setting out
the treatments and products proposed, the frequency of visits, and an estimate
of the total. Oregon State adds the obvious companion, which is to get estimates
from more than one operation and compare what i

What makes a job cost more later than it does now This is the most useful section on the page, and it is the one that argues
against our own busiest months.
Reading a quote Compare scope, not headline figures. Specifically:

Where money actually gets wasted Worth listing, because these are the recurring ways people spend without buying
anything.

What we do about all of this We quote from the property, and the assessment is free for everything except bed
bug verification, which is a paid confirmation visit credited toward the work if
you go ahead.

title: What Integrated Pest Management Actually Means
sections:
The phrase that stopped meaning anything Ask any pest control company in this county whether they practice integrated
pest management and the answer will be yes. Ask what it means on their jobs and
you will usually get a description of a quarterly perimeter spray with a web
sweep attached, plus a sentence about using the least amount of product
necessary.

What the definition actually says Start with the EPA, because it is the source everyone in the trade gestures at
and almost nobody quotes.

Identification is not a formality This is where most jobs are won or lost, and it is the step that gets skipped
most often because it costs time and produces no invoice line.

Monitoring, and an honest word about it Monitoring means knowing what is happening rather than assuming. In practice it
is sticky traps in the places insects travel, snap traps or tracking patches set
and then read, a record of where activity was seen and when, and comparing this
visit to the last one.

Thresholds, which is the uncomfortable part The action threshold is the piece of IPM that pest control companies quietly
drop, because it is the piece that says some level of pest presence does not
warrant a treatment.

The hierarchy, and why it is in that order Every source above orders the tools the same way, and the order is not
sentimental. It runs from most durable to least.

Where chemicals fit, precisely The last step is not a lesser step. When the threshold is crossed, treating
properly matters, and doing it narrowly is what makes the difference.
What this looks like on a job here Abstractions are cheap. Here is the shape of three actual local jobs.
How to tell whether you are getting it Six checks, all of which you can apply from your own kitchen.

The technical reason repetition fails There is an argument for this method that has nothing to do with values, and it
is the one that persuades people who find the environmental case unconvincing.

Why the climate here sharpens all of this The method matters more in Whatcom County than it would in a dry place, and the
reason is that so much of what we deal with is a moisture problem wearing an
insect costume.

Two claims to be skeptical of **"We use an IPM-based approach."** So does everyone, by their own account. The
phrase carries no information. The follow-up question that does carry
information is: what did the last job you ran here involve that was not an
application?

Where we fall short of the ideal A page that describes a standard and then implies the writer meets it perfectly
is worth very little, so here is the gap.

title: Who Pays for Pest Control in a WA Rental
sections:
The question behind the question Almost nobody calls us to ask about the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act. They
call because there are rats in the crawlspace and a disagreement about who is
paying, and the disagreement has been going for three weeks while the rats have
not stopped.

What the statute says The relevant provision is **RCW 59.18.060(4)**, part of the list of landlord
duties in the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act. It requires a landlord to:
The single-family carve-out, and what it does not do This is the part that surprises people, and it cuts both ways.

"Caused by the tenant" The other exception. The statute does not define it, and the honest answer is
that it is fact-specific and gets decided case by case rather than by a pest
control company.

Bed bugs are their own situation Bed bugs come up more than anything else in rental disputes, and they are worth
separating out for two reasons.

What Bellingham's rental program does and does not cover Inside Bellingham city limits there is a second layer, and it is commonly
misunderstood, so here is what it actually is.
If you are the tenant Practical steps, in order, none of which requires a lawyer to begin.
If you are the landlord Also practical, and mostly about arithmetic.

The parts of the building that decide this Since the single-family analysis and a large share of the multi-unit arguments
both end up pointing at the structure, it is worth being concrete about which
parts of a building are usually the reason a pest got in. These are the items a
tenant can reasonably raise as repairs and a landlord can reasonably close once.
A note on timing There is a seasonal shape to this that neither party usually factors in.
If you are neither, and just live next door One situation that fits nowhere else and comes up often enough to mention.

What we will and will not do We will come out, work out what is actually happening, find where it is getting
in, and put the findings and the recommended work in writing in a form either
party can hand to the other. That document describes the building and the work.
It is not a determination of liability and it does not pretend to be one.

Where to go for the actual legal answer Repeating this because it matters: the above is our reading of published rules,
linked below with the date we read them. It is not legal advice and your
situation may turn on facts we know nothing about.

title: Why Crawlspaces Here Stay Wet
sections:
The void that is actually a system Most people think of a crawlspace as leftover space — the gap between the ground
and the floor, containing pipes, and otherwise of no interest.

What the code actually requires Washington amends the model code here, and the difference matters — a
contractor working from the national figure will get it wrong.
Where the water comes from Four sources, in rough order of volume.

Why this climate is different Advice written for other regions does not transfer, and the reasons are worth
stating.
What "too wet" actually means Numbers are more useful than adjectives here.

What we find, in order of frequency **A ground cover that is missing, torn, or in unlapped pieces.** By some margin
the most common. Frequently it was installed decades ago, has been walked on by
every trade since, and now covers perhaps half the ground in fragments.

The order in which to fix it The sequence matters, because doing these out of order means doing some of them
twice.

Reading your own crawlspace You do not need a technician to form a view. What you need is a good light,
knee pads, old clothes, and about twenty minutes.

The economics, plainly People ask what this is worth spending, so here is the shape of it rather than
a number we would have to keep updating.

Should you seal it instead The sealed or conditioned crawlspace is a legitimate approach with real
advantages, and it is also the thing most often done badly.

Two myths worth retiring **"The vents should be closed in winter to save heat."** This is the most common
piece of bad advice in circulation locally, and it is usually given with real
confidence. The heat saved is small; the moisture trapped is not. Ground vapor
does not stop being produced because the weather turned cold, and with the
openings blocked it has nowhere to go but into the framing abo
What lives in a wet one Briefly, because this is where our part starts.

What we will tell you We look at the crawlspace properly on essentially every visit — the whole length
with a light, probing the sill plate and rim joist rather than glancing at them
— because on the housing stock here that is where the explanation usually is.

title: Pest Control in Acme, WA
sections:
One road, one river, and the valley between them Acme is not laid out like a town. It is a stretch of Highway 9 — the Valley
Highway — with working farms strung along it, a school, a fire station, and a
scattering of houses and acreage running back toward the hills on either side.
North of it is Van Zandt. South of it are Clipper and Wickersham. Together they
make up the South Fork Valley, and the

The river is what makes this different Plenty of rural Whatcom County is farmland against forest. Deming is, sixteen
miles north of here on the other fork. Custer is open country. What Acme has
that neither of those has in the same measure is a river running the whole
length of the community, close to the buildings, on a floor that does not drain
quickly.

Damp crawlspaces, and why the roof is not the answer The single most common thing we find under a house in this valley is a wet
crawlspace with a perfectly sound roof above it.

What the river corridor sends, and when Most residential rodent work in Whatcom County is house mice. In the South Fork
Valley we see a great deal of rat work alongside it, and the distinction is
worth making before anybody sets a trap, because the two animals do not behave
the same way.

When the river comes up High water is a normal feature of life here rather than an exceptional one, and
it produces a pest problem with a shape worth knowing about in advance.

Carpenter ants, and the timber on the other side The forest on the valley walls does what forest does everywhere in this county:
it maintains a very large number of carpenter ant colonies that have nothing to
do with anybody's house until they expand.

The autumn wave From late September the valley produces the same set of visitors it produces
every year, and they arrive together.
Two kinds of building, two different jobs Property here splits fairly cleanly, and the split predicts the work.

Wasps, and the ones that matter Yellowjackets in this valley are mostly a late-summer problem and mostly an
outdoor one, and the nests that cause real trouble are the ones nobody can see.

What we would rather you did not pay us for A fair amount of what gets sold as pest control in a valley like this one is
really moisture work wearing a different hat, and it is worth saying which is
which before anybody quotes you.

Getting service out here The honest limitation is scheduling rather than distance. Twenty-five miles
southeast puts Acme on route days rather than in the same-day rotation, and we
would rather tell you that up front than take a booking we cannot honor.

title: Pest Control in Alger, WA
sections:
Living against the forest Alger sits in the foothills where the freeway climbs away from the Samish
valley, and it is the top of our Skagit run — close enough to Bellingham to be
an easy part of a route we are already driving.

Carpenter ants, which are the defining problem There is more cedar and more weathered wood per property here than anywhere else
on our Skagit run, and carpenter ants follow it.
Rodents off the treeline The second constant, and the reason exclusion matters more here than treatment.

Outbuildings, and being honest about them Nearly every property here has a shop, a barn, a garage or a run of storage
buildings, and the honest position on those is worth stating plainly.

Firewood, and why we always mention it Wood heat is common out here and firewood storage is the single most overlooked
pest factor on a rural property.

Spiders and centipedes The heaviest pressure of anywhere on our Skagit run, and for a straightforward
reason — damp wooded ground produces insects in quantity, and spiders follow the
food.

Wasps on acreage Worth its own note because on rural property this is a safety issue rather than
a nuisance one.

Wells, septic and the damp-building list Most property out here is on a well and a septic system, and both are worth
mentioning.

The Alger year **Winter.** Rodents indoors, and the damage from the autumn becoming visible.
Firewood brings the occasional startling spider into a warm room.

What we will not sell you **Anything living that is not an insect or a rodent.** On a wooded lot the
question comes up constantly — something in the attic, something under the deck,
something on the roof at night. Insects and rodents are ours; wildlife belongs
to a specialist, and we will tell you which one you have.

The crawlspace, and why we always go under On rural acreage the crawlspace is where the answer is, and it is the step most
commonly skipped by whoever came before us.

Wells, water and what it means for the work Most property here is on a well and a septic system, and both change how we
approach a site.

What the season does to access Worth mentioning because it affects planning more than people expect on wooded
acreage.

How we work in Alger Alger sits on scheduled route days rather than same-day availability, though
being on the corridor makes it one of the easier Skagit addresses for us to
reach. Mention your driveway when you call if it is a difficult one — it changes
what we can bring.

title: Pest Control in Bellingham, WA
sections:
One city, a dozen different jobs Bellingham looks like a single market on a map and behaves like several. The
city grew outward and upward in distinct waves, and each wave left behind a
different way of failing. A house on the north flats and a house on Alabama Hill
are three miles apart and have almost nothing in common from our side of the
work. We do not treat them the same, and the first thing

The neighborhoods, grouped by what actually happens in them The City recognizes twenty-five neighborhoods. From a pest standpoint they sort
into about six groups, and knowing which group an address falls in tells you
most of what you need to know before the truck arrives.

Rats, and the specifically Bellingham version of the problem Norway rats are the most common single reason a Bellingham household calls a
pest company, and the local pattern is worth understanding because it is not the
one described in national material.
Ants in a city built on wet ground Two ants matter here and they are commonly confused.

The fall spider season Every September the phone starts ringing about large fast spiders indoors, and
every year the answer is the same and reassuring. These are almost always giant
house spiders, which are established throughout western Washington, are harmless
to people, and are not moving indoors because it is getting cold. Adult males
are wandering because they are looking for mates, and the o

Wasps, hornets and the Bellingham summer Yellowjackets are the main event, and they turn up in three places with
predictable regularity: in the ground along the edge of lawns and greenbelts, in
wall voids entered through a gap in the siding or a failed vent screen, and in
soffits and eaves on the sunny side of a house.
Cockroaches, and where they actually live Worth being specific about, because the work goes where the insects are.

How we actually work here We are based on the Guide Meridian, which puts every Bellingham neighborhood
inside a short drive, and it is why city addresses are usually a day or two and
why an active wasp nest or a rodent in living space can often be handled faster
than that.

title: Alabama Hill Pest Control — Bellingham
sections:
A neighborhood that aged all at once Alabama Hill went up in a concentrated period through the 1960s and 70s, on
sloping ground east of the city, and that shared birthday is the single most
useful fact about working here.

The cedar, and what fifty years does to it Cedar was used generously here and it is the material that most defines our work
on this hill.

Components at end of life Beyond the cedar, this era left a specific inventory, and most of it is now on
borrowed time.

What the slope does Alabama Hill is built into a grade and the terrain shapes the building envelope
more than people expect.

Landscaping that grew up Everything on this hill was planted small in about 1970, and almost none of it
is small now.

The wooded edge Parts of the hill back onto trees, and where they do the pressure is different in
degree rather than in kind.

Rodents and the autumn The seasonal logic here is the Bellingham one, sharpened by the hillside and the
housing age.

Insulation, and what a winter costs On a hill with this much rodent pressure it is worth being specific about what
happens inside a building over a season.

The renovation moment A great many houses on this hill are being updated, and renovation is the best
and worst time for this work.

Wasps on a hillside Banked ground, terracing and retaining structures give yellowjackets the cavities
they want, and a ground nest beside a set of steps or a path is invisible until
somebody disturbs it. On a property where people are walking narrow paths between
levels that is a genuine hazard, and the colony peaks in late summer when
everybody is outdoors.

Spiders, and the September phone call Giant house spiders bring the autumn calls. They are harmless, they have been
established across western Washington for generations, and the big fast ones
found indoors are wandering males looking for mates rather than anything coming
in for warmth. A spider stranded in a bath is a male that got in and could not
climb out.

What we will not sell you **A promise about the treeline.** That population is permanent. We seal the
building, which is the part that actually works.

How a visit works here We start outside, and on this hill that walk takes a while. Every elevation where
the building meets earth, the drainage and where it discharges, the condition of
the cedar at its edges and joints, the deck and its ledger, the vent screens, the
soffit line, the branches reaching the roof, the stumps and dead wood on the lot,
the firewood, and the retaining structures.

Buying or selling on the hill A short note, because the housing stock here turns over steadily and the same
findings come up in transaction after transaction.

title: Barkley Pest Control — Bellingham, WA
sections:
Density without age Barkley is an unusual thing to work in, because it combines two conditions that
normally arrive separately.

The building is one system A modern podium building — concrete at the base, wood frame above, uses stacked
vertically — is efficient to construct precisely because it shares things.

Refuse rooms and chutes If there is one thing that decides rodent outcomes in this neighborhood, it is
the waste system, and it is nothing like a household bin.

Restaurants under homes Ground-floor food service with residential above is the defining Barkley
arrangement and it produces a specific dynamic.

Structured and underground parking Parking beneath or within these buildings is the part nobody thinks of as part
of the building, and it is worth naming.

Landscaping designed to look finished Barkley was planted to look established from the day it opened, and the planting
is denser and closer to the buildings than in an older neighborhood where things
grew in gradually.

Townhomes and the shared wall The townhome stock here shares one wall or two, which puts it between a house
and an apartment building in how problems behave.
What the buildings do well Worth saying, because it is true and it changes what we recommend.

Wasps and the balconies Newer construction produces more wasp work than older stock, and Barkley
concentrates it.

Deliveries, and the cardboard problem A dense residential building receives an enormous volume of parcels, and the
packaging is a genuine factor rather than a trivial one.

What we will not sell you **A single-unit treatment presented as a building fix.** Where the population is
shared, we say so before taking the work rather than after the third visit.

How we work here For a building we start with the manager or the association: how many units,
which are affected, what connects them, where the waste goes, who maintains the
landscaping, and what the parking arrangement is. That conversation takes twenty
minutes and it determines whether the program resolves anything.

Offices, clinics and the daytime tenancies The professional space here — medical and dental practices, offices, studios and
therapy rooms — sits in the same buildings as everything above, and it has its
own constraints worth naming.

The seasons in a dense building The annual pattern here differs from a detached house in one important respect:
much of the pressure is internal and does not follow the weather at all.

title: City Center Pest Control — Bellingham
sections:
The block is the unit There is one fact that governs pest work in downtown Bellingham, and most people
leasing a unit here have never been told it: **the buildings are joined.**

Mixed use, and the vertical dimension Downtown adds a complication that a purely commercial district does not have:
people live here, frequently directly above the businesses.

Restaurants and food service Downtown has a high density of kitchens, and food service in older buildings is
a genuinely specific discipline.

The alleys Downtown alleys are the service corridor for the entire district and they are
where a great deal of the population actually lives.

Basements, and what is under downtown Downtown Bellingham has more below-grade space than most people realize, and it
is frequently the least-visited part of a building.

Parking structures The multi-level parking downtown deserves a specific note because it is nobody's
priority and it affects everything near it.

Apartments above the shops Residential downtown is a substantial and growing share of the district, and
multi-unit work follows the same logic as the commercial side.
Rodents, and the downtown autumn The seasonal pattern is the city's, concentrated by the density.

Roofs and service plant Worth its own note because on downtown buildings this is where problems
originate and nobody looks.

What we will not sell you **A block solution from a single-tenancy contract.** If the population is
shared, we will say that plainly before taking the work.

How we work downtown For a business we start with your operating constraints — trading hours, service
times, access, what may be placed where, and any audit or record requirement —
because those shape everything after them.

Stored product, retail and back-of-house Not every downtown business is a kitchen, and the non-food premises have their
own recurring issue that gets misread as a building problem.
Vacancy between tenancies Downtown turns over, and an empty unit behaves differently from an occupied one.

title: Cordata Pest Control — Bellingham, WA
sections:
New buildings, old ground Cordata is the newest large piece of Bellingham, and it produces a conversation
we have more often here than anywhere else in the city: a homeowner who cannot
understand how a house built five years ago has rodents.

Where a tight building actually leaks Modern construction here is sound until a trade puts a hole through it. Every
penetration is drilled by a subcontractor working at pace, and the standard
closure is expanding foam.

Landscaping is the other half Newer neighborhoods are landscaped to a standard older ones are not, and the
landscaping is doing more pest work than most residents realize.

The open ground behind the fence Cordata still has undeveloped parcels, greenways, retention ponds and
agricultural land at its edges, and properties backing onto any of those are on
a different footing from those in the middle of a finished phase.

Apartment complexes A large share of Cordata is purpose-built rental housing, much of it near the
college, and multi-unit work follows different rules from a single house.

Refuse in a managed building If there is one physical change that moves rodent outcomes in this neighborhood,
it is the shared refuse area.

Wasps and newer construction Newer neighborhoods produce more wasp work than older ones and the reasons are
structural.

Medical, office and business park Cordata carries a substantial amount of non-residential building, and those
accounts are documented programs rather than visit schedules.

The Cordata year **Winter.** Rodent activity indoors at its height, and the season when autumn
damage becomes visible: staining, chewed ducting, insulation disturbed, or a
smell that is difficult to locate.

Spiders, and the September calls Giant house spiders bring the autumn calls here as everywhere in the city. They
are harmless, they have been established across western Washington for
generations, and the large fast ones people find indoors are wandering males
searching for mates rather than anything seeking warmth.

What we will not sell you **A guarantee about the field behind your fence.** That population is permanent.
We will seal your building, which is the part that actually works.

How a visit here works For a house we start outside and work the penetrations methodically — the vent,
the bib, the line set, the electrical entry, the garage seal — then the grade and
the landscaping, then the crawlspace or the attic depending on the phase, then
inside. On a newer building that exterior walk usually finds the entire problem,
and it is quick.

Conditioned crawlspaces, and what changed The newer phases here use sealed and conditioned crawlspaces rather than the
vented ones that define most of Bellingham, and it is worth explaining what that
actually buys you, because it is genuinely better and it is not a force field.

Buying or renting somewhere new A short note for anyone moving into this neighborhood, because the useful moment
is early and almost nobody uses it.

title: Edgemoor Pest Control — Bellingham, WA
sections:
Where lot size changes the work Edgemoor is the Bellingham neighborhood where the size of a property genuinely
alters how the job is done, and it is worth being specific about why.

Carpenter ants at scale Edgemoor produces more carpenter ant work per property than anywhere else we
operate, and the reason is straightforward: the neighborhood has more of what
they want.
What a thorough search actually involves Because this comes up in quoting, it is worth setting out.

The trees themselves A point worth making plainly, because anxious homeowners sometimes reach for the
wrong solution.

Several buildings, one property Most Edgemoor addresses have more than one structure, and the outbuildings are
the single most commonly overlooked part of a scope.

A neighborhood with no single housing era Unlike the hillside neighborhoods that went up in one concentrated push, Edgemoor
has been built out across a very long period, and that has a practical
consequence.

Rodents on a wooded lot The seasonal pattern is the regional one, delivered more efficiently than it is
in town.

Water, drainage and the ground Large wooded lots handle water differently from small ones, and it produces
findings people do not expect.

Wasps on large grounds Extensive grounds mean more places for a nest and more chance of an unpleasant
discovery.

The saltwater edge The western margin of the neighborhood runs out to Chuckanut Bay, and the lots
that sit on or near that edge behave differently again from the wooded interior.

Houses that stand empty for stretches A fair number of properties here are unoccupied for weeks at a time — travel,
second residences, a season spent elsewhere. That changes the pest picture in
one specific way: nothing gets noticed early.
Discretion and access Two practical notes, because they come up here more than elsewhere.

What we will not sell you **Tree removal for an ant problem.** A healthy mature tree is very rarely the
nest, and losing one to a misdiagnosis is expensive and irreversible.

How a visit works here We start with the grounds rather than the building, which is the reverse of most
of our work and the right order on a property this size. The treeline and
understory, deadwood and stumps, fallen timber, garden and landscape structures,
the firewood, drainage and where water actually goes, and every outbuilding.

title: Fairhaven Pest Control — Bellingham, WA
sections:
A district with two halves Fairhaven is the most architecturally distinct part of Bellingham and, from our
side of the work, it is really two different jobs that happen to share a name.

The commercial core, and why the block is the unit The single most useful thing to understand about doing pest work in a historic
commercial block is that the buildings are connected, and almost nobody who
leases a unit in one knows it.

Old buildings, old openings The commercial stock here is well over a century old in places, and age brings
its own inventory of ways in.

Food service in a hundred-year-old building A good share of the district is restaurants and cafés, and it is a genuinely
specific job.

The residential streets Away from the commercial core, Fairhaven's housing is old, individual and often
substantial — a mix of turn-of-the-century houses, later infill, and a good
number of properties that have been divided into units at some point.

The creek corridor and the greenbelt Padden Creek and the wooded corridor running through the district are among the
best things about living here, and they are a permanent source of pressure.

Apartments and divided houses Fairhaven has a substantial rental stock, including older houses divided into
units and apartments above the commercial spaces, and that changes how some work
has to be scoped.
Visitors, and what the season does Fairhaven is a destination, and the seasonal swing shows up in our work.

Spiders, and the autumn calls Every September the phone starts about large fast spiders indoors, and in a
district with this much greenbelt, this much mature planting and this much old
crawlspace, the volume is high.

What we will not sell you **Anything with fur or feathers.** Birds on a parapet, an animal in a ceiling
void — none of that is ours. We do insects and rodents, and we will tell you
which you have and hand you a better number for the rest.

How a visit here works For a residential property we start outside and walk the whole perimeter,
including the greenbelt side, which is the elevation people rarely look at and
where a good share of the findings are. Grade and drainage, the
siding-to-foundation transition, vents, penetrations, vegetation contact, and
the state of any previous exclusion work. Then underneath properly with a light,
w

Buildings on the water side The properties running down toward the bay and the marine edge pick up a factor
the rest of the district does not.

Renovation, and the moment to act A great deal of this district is being restored, and renovation is
simultaneously the best and the worst time for pest work.

title: Happy Valley Pest Control — Bellingham
sections:
A turnover neighborhood Happy Valley sits below the Western campus and it is defined less by how its
buildings were built than by how often they change hands.

Turnover is the transport mechanism Bed bugs and, to a lesser extent, German cockroaches move with belongings. They
do not fly, they do not travel far under their own power, and they do not appear
spontaneously in a clean building. They arrive in things people carry.

The scope problem in shared housing This is the thing that most often goes wrong here, and it is not a treatment
failure.
Bed bugs specifically Early detection is the entire game, and the economics are stark.
German cockroaches The other signature of this neighborhood, and routinely misidentified.

The buildings themselves Underneath the turnover, Happy Valley's housing is a mix, and the stock does
matter.

Waste, and the thing landlords can actually change If there is one physical intervention that changes outcomes in this
neighborhood, it is refuse.
Rodents and the autumn The seasonal pattern is the Bellingham one, sharpened by the housing.

Spiders, and the reassuring answer Every September the calls start, and in a neighborhood that has just refilled
with people who have not lived through a Pacific Northwest autumn before, the
volume is high.

What we will not sell you **A single-unit treatment presented as a building solution.** If the population
is shared, we say so before taking the work.

How we work here Happy Valley is minutes from our shop and most calls are handled inside a couple of days, with urgent
ones faster.

Between tenancies, which is the whole opportunity Worth its own section for landlords and managers, because the single most
valuable window in this neighborhood is one that most owners spend doing
something else.

What tenants can do, and what they cannot It is worth being straight with renters, because a lot of the advice aimed at
them is either useless or unfair.

Fleas, and the pet question Worth covering because shared houses in this neighborhood turn over pets as
often as they turn over people.
Noise, damage and what a landlord actually pays for The costs in this neighborhood are rarely the treatment.

title: Irongate Pest Control — Bellingham, WA
sections:
An industrial neighborhood in a residential city Irongate is Bellingham's light industrial quarter, and almost nothing that
applies to the rest of the city applies here.

The building cannot be sealed, and that is the starting point The single most useful thing we bring to an Irongate account is refusing to
pretend otherwise.

The yard is the problem Most interior rodent activity in this neighborhood is the visible end of an
exterior population, and the exterior is almost always more habitable than the
building.

Nobody is here at night This is the factor that most distinguishes Irongate from a retail or hospitality
setting, and it cuts both ways.

Vehicles and fleet The most expensive damage we deal with in this neighborhood is almost never in a
building.

Break rooms, and the food nobody counts A recurring conversation here starts with a client saying there is no food on
site, so a rodent problem makes no sense.

Stored product and materials Where a business handles feed, seed, grain, packaged food, pet products or dry
goods of any kind, there is a second category worth separating out.

Self-storage and long-term storage There is a good deal of storage capacity in this neighborhood and it has its own
character.

Roofs, mezzanines and the spaces above Industrial buildings put a great deal of service equipment on the roof and a
great deal of storage on mezzanines, and both are under-inspected.

Documentation For most accounts here the record is a real part of the value, and it should be
built to be read by somebody other than the person who ordered the service.

What we will not sell you **A sealed industrial building.** Repeating it because it is the promise most
often made in this neighborhood and it cannot be delivered.

How we work in Irongate We start with your operating reality — hours, access, safety requirements,
whether there are areas we cannot enter, what may be placed where, and any audit
or insurance obligation. On an industrial site those constraints are the job
rather than an obstacle to it.

Wasps, and why they matter more on an industrial site Stinging insects are a safety issue in this neighborhood in a way they are not
at a house, and the reasons are specific to how these premises are used.

Water, drains and the wet corners Industrial sites supply water more generously than anyone realizes, and it is
half of what sustains a population that has no obvious food source.
Neighboring sites, and the shared perimeter One thing worth saying plainly to anyone in a business park.

title: Lettered Streets Pest Control — Bellingham
sections:
The oldest ground in the city The Lettered Streets are where Bellingham's residential history starts. This is
the oldest continuously occupied housing in the city, laid out on a tight grid
north of downtown, on small lots with alleys running behind, under mature street
trees, with a great deal of the stock predating 1930.

Post-and-pier over bare earth Most of these houses sit on posts and piers with a short crawlspace beneath, and
in a large share of them the floor of that crawlspace is still soil.
Framing that runs floor to roof The second feature is the one that produces the most baffled phone calls.

A century of penetrations The third is simple accumulation. Gas, water, waste, electrical, three
generations of telephone and cable, an abandoned oil line, a chimney thimble
from a stove nobody remembers. Every one drilled generously by whoever was doing
that job on that day, and essentially none of them sealed afterwards.

The alleys, and why the block matters This is the feature that makes the Lettered Streets different from anywhere else
in the city, and it is worth being honest about.

Rats, and the Bellingham autumn Norway rats are the most common single reason anyone in this neighborhood calls
us, and the local pattern is not the one national material describes.
Carpenter and moisture ants Both are common in this stock and the distinction changes everything.

Bed bugs and shared walls The Lettered Streets carry a substantial rental stock, including a lot of older
houses divided into units, and that changes how bed bug work has to be scoped.

Spiders, and the reassuring version Every September the calls start about large fast spiders indoors, and in
century-old housing with this much crawlspace and this much mature planting the
volume is high.

Garages, outbuildings and the back of the lot The buildings behind the house matter more here than in most neighborhoods, and
they are routinely left out of scope by whoever quoted before us.

Renovation, and what opening a wall reveals A lot of these houses are being restored, and renovation is both the best and
the worst moment for pest work.

Heating, chimneys and the winter list Older houses here have been heated several different ways over their lives and
each has left something behind.

title: Sehome Pest Control — Bellingham, WA
sections:
A forest in the middle of a city Sehome is unusual and the reason is Sehome Hill. The arboretum on top of it is
not a landscaped park with mown edges; it is a genuine second-growth forest,
several hundred acres of it, sitting in the middle of a dense residential
neighborhood with the university on one flank.

What the arboretum delivers A forest edge is a supply line. It runs continuous cover from deep habitat right
up to a building, and on an ordinary city block an animal has to cross open
ground to reach a house. Here, along the arboretum boundary, it does not.

What the slope does Steep ground changes the building envelope in ways that matter more than people
expect.
The housing, in two layers Sehome's stock divides roughly into two, and they behave differently.

Apartment buildings, and getting the scope right A good share of our Sehome work is multi-unit, and it is the situation where
scope decides the outcome more than technique does.

Refuse in a dense neighborhood If there is one physical thing that changes rodent outcomes here, it is the
refuse situation, and in a neighborhood of apartment buildings and shared houses
it compounds fast.
The autumn, and the useful window The seasonal pattern here is the Bellingham one with the forest edge added.
Ants, and reading them properly Two ants matter here and the difference decides the approach.

Spiders, and what to tell a nervous new tenant Every September the calls start, and in a neighborhood that has just refilled
with people who have not lived through a Pacific Northwest autumn before, the
volume is high and the alarm is genuine.

What we will not sell you **A single-unit treatment sold as a building solution.** If the population is
shared, we will say so before taking the work rather than after the third visit.

How a visit here works We start outside, and on a Sehome property that walk takes longer than it does
on flat ground. Every elevation where the building meets earth, the drainage and
where it discharges, the retaining walls and terracing, the deck and its ledger,
the vents and penetrations, the branches reaching the roof, and the forest
boundary if there is one.

Wasps, and the hillside problem Wasps are worth their own note here because the terrain changes where they nest
and how dangerous that is.

Insulation, and what the autumn leaves behind On a neighborhood with this much rodent pressure it is worth setting out what
actually happens inside a building over a winter.

title: Silver Beach Pest Control — Bellingham
sections:
A summer place that stayed Silver Beach runs along the Bellingham end of Lake Whatcom, and a great deal of
it began as somewhere to spend July rather than somewhere to live.

Working inside the catchment Lake Whatcom is the drinking water source for the city and much of the
surrounding area, and Silver Beach sits directly on it.

What the original construction left The converted-cabin stock shares a set of characteristics, and every one is a
pest consideration once a building is occupied through a wet winter.
Steep lots and the water problem Silver Beach falls to the lake, and slope decides where the trouble is.

Cedar, and the carpenter ant problem There is a great deal of cedar in this neighborhood and it is old enough to
matter.

The wooded side Where the neighborhood backs onto wooded ground rather than water, it behaves
like forest edge.
Docks, boathouses and stored gear Worth its own note because they are common here and routinely left out of scope.
The lake, the insects and the evenings Living on water changes the insect load in a way that surprises new residents.

The autumn, and the right window The seasonal pattern is the Bellingham one with the wooded and lakeside supply
added.

Spiders and the September calls They are giant house spiders. Harmless, long established across western
Washington, and the large fast ones people find are wandering males looking for
mates rather than anything moving in for warmth. The ones stranded in a bath are
males that got in and could not climb back out.

What we will not sell you **Broadcast applications on the lake side.** In a drinking water catchment that
is the wrong tool, and we would rather quote exclusion and habitat correction
even where it is a smaller job.

How a visit here works We start outside and the walk takes a while on these lots. Every elevation where
the building meets earth, the drainage and where it actually discharges, the
condition of the cedar, the deck and its ledger, the skirting and underfloor
access, the stumps and standing dead wood, the firewood, the branches over the
roof, and the outbuildings and anything near the water.

Ants that are not carpenter ants Two other ants turn up here regularly and both get misidentified as the
expensive one.

Seasonal and part-time occupancy A number of properties here are second homes, family places used at weekends, or
lettings that run heavily in summer and sit quiet through the winter, and the
occupancy pattern changes the risk.

title: Whatcom Falls Pest Control — Bellingham
sections:
The neighborhood is defined by its edge Whatcom Falls is named for the park, and the park is not a detail of the
neighborhood. It is the organizing fact of it.

Why this is an exclusion neighborhood In most of Bellingham a pest problem has a source you can do something about. A
