The first autumn in a new house The first autumn is when people find out what their house does, and on the
edge of open ground it is a busy one.

Heat pumps and modern mechanicals Houses here carry equipment that older housing does not, and it introduces
routes nobody thinks to check.

What the corridor will become Worth thinking about now rather than in ten years: the restored corridor is
designed to improve as habitat, and it will.

Buying new here: what to ask before you sign People move into this area straight from a builder, and there are three
questions worth asking that nobody thinks to ask.

Wasps in new soffits Wasps in new-construction soffits are a real pattern and this is where it
shows.

Dust, disturbance and the first two years One more thing about living beside active work, and it is the part people find
hardest to plan for: the pressure does not arrive once and settle. It arrives
every time the ground moves.

What is worth doing, in order On a house here the ranking is unusually clear and most of it is not a
treatment.

What we would rather not sell you A recurring perimeter program on a two-year-old house whose actual problem is a
foamed line set and a garage door gap will produce a visible result forever and
will never finish.

How a visit works here We start with the surroundings, because on this ground they are the whole
story: what is being worked, what is being built, how close the creek buffer or
the stormwater margin gets, and what state the ground next door is in.

title: Sterling Meadows Pest Control — Lynden, WA
sections:
New housing on the south edge Sterling Meadows is newer subdivision housing on the south side of Lynden,
built over a short period to a consistent specification, on ground that was
agricultural before it was residential.

Tight is not sealed New construction is excellent at what it was designed for. It is airtight to a
standard older housing never approached, it manages water intelligently, and it
is insulated properly.

The warranty question, worth asking early On housing of this age some of what we find may not be a maintenance item at
all.

One era, one set of details, one advantage Almost everything about a single-period development is a disadvantage for
character and a considerable advantage for diagnosis.
Ground that was farmed, and ground that still is Land does not stop being what it was because it has houses on it now.

Drainage on former farm ground Development on agricultural land inherits the drainage that was there, and it
is worth a look on a property of this age.

Landscaping: the window that is open now Right now the planting here is young, set back and open, and on most of these
houses the foundation line can be seen and reached the whole way round.

Heat pumps, line sets and modern mechanicals Houses here carry equipment older housing does not, and it introduces routes
and harborage nobody thinks to check.

The first autumn, and every one after From late September the sunny elevations collect the seasonal crowd, and on the
edge of open ground there is nothing to intercept them.

Wasps in the soffits Modern soffit and fascia detailing creates long continuous voids with small
openings at intervals — vents, joints, the end of a run at a gable — which is
precisely what a queen is looking for in spring. They are twenty feet up,
invisible from the ground, and nobody inspects them.

Families, pets and how work gets placed This is family housing with children and dogs in the yards, and that shapes
placement rather than possibility.

What is worth doing, in order Close the builder gaps first: penetrations done mechanically rather than with
foam alone, vent screening fixed into the opening, and the garage door seal.
It takes a morning, and it does most of the work.

Fence lines, and what collects along them On lots this size the boundary between two properties is one of the more
productive things to look at, and almost nobody does.

What we would rather not sell you A recurring perimeter program on a five-year-old house whose real problem is a
foamed line set and a garage door gap will produce a visible result forever and
will never finish.

When the street is worth doing together Because every house here shares a specification, this is one of the few places
where doing several at once is genuinely better rather than merely cheaper.

How a visit works here We start outside at ground level, and on housing this uniform we largely know
what we are looking for before we arrive: the foundation line, every service
penetration including the line set, vent screening and how it is fixed, sweeps
and thresholds, and the garage door corners from the inside with the door shut.

title: Pest Control in Mount Vernon, WA
sections:
The county seat, and three towns inside it Mount Vernon is the largest place we work south of the county line, and like
most towns of its age it is really several places sharing a name. From our side
of the work there are three, and the address tells you which one you are in
before anything else does.

Downtown, where the problem belongs to the block Mount Vernon has a real historic core — masonry and timber commercial buildings,
many over a century old, built shoulder to shoulder.
Food service in old buildings A good share of the downtown is food service, and it is a specific job.

The river and the low ground The Skagit is a serious river with a long flood history, and Mount Vernon sits
against it behind a dike and floodwall system.

The older residential stock Away from downtown, the older Mount Vernon housing carries the standard Pacific
Northwest pattern and it is the same pattern we deal with in Bellingham's
prewar neighborhoods.

The new edges, and the farmland behind them Mount Vernon has grown outward, and the newer subdivisions sit against
agricultural ground.
Ants, and what they are telling you Two ants matter here and they get confused constantly.

The year in Mount Vernon **Winter.** Indoor rodent activity peaks, since whatever got in during autumn has not left. Damage becomes visible — soiled insulation,
chewed ducting, a stain in a ceiling, a smell in a room that turns out to be
something dead in a cavity.

Spiders, and the autumn phone calls Every September the calls start about large fast spiders indoors, and the answer
is reassuring rather than alarming.

Cockroaches, and where they actually live Worth being specific about, because the treatment only works where the insects
actually are.

What we will not sell you **Anything that is not an insect or a rodent.** Birds on a downtown parapet, an animal in a ceiling void, a bat in an attic — none of that is ours. Sasquatch does pest control and exclusion, and we would rather send you to the right operator on the first call than take a booking we cannot serve.

Multi-unit and rental housing Mount Vernon has a substantial rental and apartment stock, and multi-unit work
follows different rules from a single house.

How we work here Mount Vernon sits on scheduled route days rather than same-day availability,
because it is a genuine drive from our base in Bellingham. We will tell you
which day that puts you on rather than promise a window we cannot hold, and if
something is urgent — a nest by a door, a rodent in living space — say so and we
will do what we can.

title: Pest Control in Nooksack, WA
sections:
The town is small and the ground around it is not Nooksack has fewer than two thousand residents and covers less than a square mile.
Almost everything that decides pest pressure here happens outside that square mile,
in the berry fields, the dairy ground and the open country that runs from the edge
of town to the foothills.

Berry ground, and what harvest does to it Whatcom County grows more red raspberries than anywhere else in the country, and
Nooksack sits in the middle of that. Raspberry and blueberry acreage surrounds the
town on most sides, along with the dairy and grass ground mixed through it.

What that looks like at a building The first structures to take it are the ones nearest the field and least sealed:
equipment sheds, detached shops, pump houses, barns and older outbuildings. Those
buildings frequently have gaps that nobody minds, because until now nothing was
using them.

Cluster flies, and why they concentrate here Cluster flies are one of the defining rural pests of this part of the county, and
Nooksack gets them heavily.

Stink bugs and Asian lady beetles do the same thing The brown marmorated stink bug and the multicolored Asian lady beetle follow the
same pattern on the same walls at roughly the same time, and the three are
routinely found together.

The overwintering window is short The reason we push people to plan this in August rather than October is that the
window is genuinely narrow.

Everson is a mile away and this is not that page Nooksack and Everson sit about a mile apart and share a school district, a valley
and a good deal of housing stock. It would be easy to write the same page twice.
Carpenter ants and moisture ants The ant work here follows the buildings rather than the fields.
Wasps on a rural property Wasps are worse on acreage than in town, for two straightforward reasons.

Spiders and the rest of the domestic list Spiders are the most common thing people ask about and among the least dangerous.
No spider of medical concern has an established population in Whatcom County. Giant
house spiders and cross orbweavers account for most of what turns up, and the
autumn surge indoors is males wandering to find females rather than an invasion.

Feed rooms, coolers and the small commercial side A fair share of the work around Nooksack is not residential at all. Berry and
dairy operations run buildings that concentrate exactly what rodents want: feed
in bulk, water, warmth and constant door movement.

What actually holds on a rural building Exclusion on acreage fails in predictable ways, and most of them come down to
material choice.

Rodents in the attic, and what you are actually hearing Most rural rodent calls start with a noise, and the noise tells you more than
people expect.

The Nooksack year **January to March.** Overwintering insects waking in wall voids and appearing
indoors on warm days. Rodents already established and now breeding. This is
cleanup and exclusion season rather than prevention season.

What we will not sell you **A monthly contract for a house with no ongoing pressure.** Plenty of properties
here have a real, continuous problem because of what surrounds them. Plenty do
not. If a one-time treatment and some sealing will hold, we will say so.

How we work in Nooksack Nooksack is eighteen miles from the shop and it sits on scheduled route days.
Most calls in Whatcom County are handled within one to two days, and about three
across August and September when everybody phones at once. We would rather name
the day than promise a window we cannot keep.

title: Pest Control in Sedro-Woolley, WA
sections:
A mill town, and what that left behind Sedro-Woolley grew as a mill and railroad town, and the housing stock reflects
exactly that history. A dense core of worker housing built for people employed
within walking distance, laid out on small lots, much of it going up between
roughly 1900 and 1950, with a compact commercial downtown at the center and the
valley opening out around it.

The housing, and how it fails Older Sedro-Woolley housing shares a set of characteristics that were entirely
sensible when they were built and are a straightforward invitation now.

Carpenter ants, the local signature If there is one insect that defines older Sedro-Woolley property, this is it,
and the reason is simply age.

Moisture ants, and reading them correctly Moisture ants get confused with carpenter ants constantly and the message they
carry is different.

Wood-boring beetles and decay Damp crawlspaces in old housing produce two things people find alarming and
frequently misread.

Downtown and the connected block Sedro-Woolley has a compact commercial core of older buildings, many sharing
walls.

The river corridor The Skagit runs along the town and the dike and drainage system that manages it
runs with it.

The eastern edge and the forest East of town the valley climbs and the character changes to forest edge, and a
good share of the housing out that way is cedar against standing timber.

Firewood, and why it matters here Wood heat is common in this part of the county and firewood storage is one of
the most reliably overlooked pest factors on a property.

The year here **Winter.** Rodent activity indoors at its height, and the season when the
autumn's damage becomes obvious: soiled insulation, chewed ducting, a stain in a
ceiling, a smell that turns out to be something dead in a cavity. Firewood
brings the occasional startling spider indoors.

What we will not sell you **Anything with fur or feathers.** Birds, bats, squirrels, raccoons and other
wildlife are outside what we do. We handle insects and rodents, and we will tell
you which you have and who to call for the rest.

Spiders, and the reassuring answer Every autumn the calls start about large fast spiders indoors, and in a town
with this much old housing and this much wooded ground nearby the load is
genuinely heavy.

title: Pest Control in Sudden Valley, WA
sections:
Cedar, slope and forest Sudden Valley is one of the most distinctive places we work, and its pest
profile follows directly from three facts about how it was built.
Carpenter ants, which are the signature problem If Sudden Valley has one defining pest, this is it.

Mice, and why there are so many Carpenter ants are the signature problem here, and mice are the volume one.
Sudden Valley is houses set into standing woodland, and mouse pressure off
woodland is a different order of magnitude from mouse pressure in a town — there
is no edge to push back, because the forest starts at the deck. Deer mice come
in off the trees and the ground cover, and they arrive in

The watershed, which constrains everything Sudden Valley sits in the Lake Whatcom catchment, and Lake Whatcom is the
drinking water reservoir for Bellingham and much of the surrounding area. A
great deal of this community drains toward it.
What the slope and the construction do Steep lots change the building envelope in ways that matter.

Working within the association Sudden Valley is a covenanted community with an association, and exterior work
frequently needs approval — vent covers, screening, netting, chimney caps and
anything else that changes how a building looks from outside.

Wasps and stinging insects on wooded lots Wooded, sloped property generates a particular wasp problem and it is worth
understanding before somebody meets it with a mower.

The Sudden Valley year **Winter.** Rodent activity indoors at its height, and the season when attic and
crawlspace damage from the autumn becomes obvious — soiled insulation, chewed
ducting, a stain in a ceiling.

Rodents and the underfloor question Rodent work here has its own character because of how the houses sit on the
ground.

Wet crawlspaces on sloped ground This is the underlying condition beneath a large share of what we get called
about here, and it is worth treating as its own subject.
Access, and what it changes Worth mentioning because it affects scheduling more than people expect.

What we will not sell you **Wildlife of any kind.** Up here the call comes in all the time: a noise in the attic, something living under the deck, footsteps on the roof after dark. Our answer is the same every time: insects and rodents are ours, everything else belongs to a wildlife operator, and we will tell you which you have.

How we work here Sudden Valley is about eight miles from our shop, though the last stretch is
slower than the map suggests. Most calls are handled inside a day or two.

title: Pest Control in Sumas, WA
sections:
A small town with a large front door Sumas has a very small population and an international land border crossing, and
that combination produces a pest profile out of all proportion to its size.

Freight, warehousing and the commercial side Goods arrive from somewhere else, and whatever traveled with them arrives too.
That is the fundamental fact of pest work anywhere freight concentrates, and it
is why a warehouse in Sumas has an exposure that a house a mile away does not.

Flood recovery Sumas took severe flood damage in November 2021, and a large share of the
town's buildings have been through inundation and rebuilding since. That history
is still the most important thing about many of these structures from our point
of view.

Farm ground on every side The agricultural work around Sumas is the same trade as the rest of the north
county, at a scale between Everson and Lynden.

Stink bugs and Asian lady beetles Both are overwintering insects rather than a structural problem, and both are a
real and recurring Sumas call. They gather on sunlit walls in autumn — south and
west faces, warm afternoons — and then work into the building through the same
small gaps everything else uses. The important thing to know is that once they
are inside a wall void, treating them there is

The residential town The housing in Sumas is a small-town mix, with the added complication that much
of it has been repaired or rebuilt in the last few years.
Carpenter ants and moisture ants Both are common here and the distinction matters.

The Sumas year **Winter.** Interior rodent work and damage assessment, in houses and in
commercial buildings alike. On rebuilt property this is when the gaps left by a
hurried repair start showing themselves.

What we will not sell you **Bird work or wildlife removal.** Businesses under time pressure ask, and the answer does not change: it is not what we do. We will say so on the phone and point you to somebody who handles it rather than taking the booking.

Stored-product insects Worth its own section here, because a town with warehousing sees these more than
a town without one, and because they are routinely misdiagnosed.

Spiders and the domestic list The household side of Sumas is the standard regional set. Giant house spiders
generate the autumn calls and are harmless — the large fast ones are wandering
males, not an invasion, and there is no brown recluse in this state's northwest
corner. Silverfish, sowbugs and millipedes belong to the damp crawl and are
reporting a moisture condition rather than a pest problem

Ants in a town that has been rebuilt Carpenter and moisture ants are worth a second look here because the rebuild
history changes where they turn up.
Spiders and the seasonal domestic list The household calendar here is the standard regional one.

Moisture, and why it is the recurring theme Almost everything on this page traces back to water, which is worth stating
plainly.

How we work in Sumas Sumas is about twenty-three miles out, with the last stretch on two-lane road
shared with farm and truck traffic, so it sits on scheduled route days rather
than same-day availability. We will tell you which day that means rather than
promise a window we cannot keep.

title: Aerial Yellowjacket: The Paper Nest in the Shrub
sections:
The species in the middle Whatcom County has two famous wasps and one that does most of its work without a
name anybody uses.

What it is A yellowjacket, in the strict sense — same subfamily, same enclosed paper
architecture, same annual colony. WSU Hortsense lists it among the state's
common social wasps as one of the species with relatively stout bodies and
distinct yellow and black banded coloring.

The nest, and why it will not settle the question An envelope of gray paper wrapped around several tiers of comb, with the way in
at the bottom. [UC IPM](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7450.html)'s description of the aerial nesters covers both species at
once — paper nests attached to the eaves of a building or hanging from the limb
of a tree, with the entrance normally a hole at the bottom

The first mistake: calling it a hornet Somebody sees the paper nest, calls it a hornet nest, and adjusts their behavior
to match a reputation.
The second mistake: hunting for a hole in the lawn This one costs more, and we hear it several times a year.

Where it puts the nest The Northeastern IPM Center's observation is the important one for this county:
this species will build in voids as well as trees, and in closer proximity to
human activity than its relatives. That is the difference that matters, and it
is why an aerial yellowjacket nest is more likely than a bald-faced hornet nest
to be somewhere that forces the issue.

How it behaves, near the nest and away from it Near the nest, this is not a species to take liberties with. UC IPM's language
for the aerial nesters is that they are extremely defensive when their nests are
disturbed, and it adds a detail specific to this one that is worth carrying
around: defending individuals of *D. arenaria* sometimes bite and sting
simultaneously.

It is not the wasp at your table UC IPM draws a line between the two groups of yellowjackets that almost nobody
outside the field knows about: the aerial nesters do not become scavengers at
the end of the season.

Watching a nest from the ground Once a paper nest has been found, almost every question worth asking about it
can be answered from thirty feet away with no equipment and no risk. It is worth
doing before anybody decides anything, because the answers change the
recommendation.
The year, and what happens to the nest One season, start to finish, like everything else in this group.

Nest position is what decides the job This profile carries a verdict of *depends*, and it is the same verdict as its
two relatives for the same reason: the species is not what decides. Position is.
Sort the nest into one of these and the answer follows.

What the work involves Enclosed nests are treated as a unit, and the details differ from the
ground-nest method more than people expect.

Reducing the odds next year None of this involves treating anything, and all of it works better than
anything that does.

Around the county **Sudden Valley, Geneva and the Lake Whatcom shore.** Mature ornamental
plantings run into native cover, and the shrub nest is the local version — found
by somebody clearing an overgrown boundary in August.

Related work The full seasonal picture and how the work is scheduled sit on
[wasp and hornet control](/services/wasp-control/). The black and white relative
that builds the same kind of nest is the
[bald-faced hornet](/pest-library/bald-faced-hornet/), and the aerial nest in a
tree is covered in detail on
[bald-faced hornet nest in a tree](/services/wasp-control/bald-faced-hornet-nest-in-a-tree/).

title: Anobiid Powderpost Beetle in Whatcom County
sections:
The name on the page is the wrong name Almost everything written about this insect online is written about a different
family, and the mix-up is not trivial — it points people at the wrong wood, the
wrong buildings and the wrong remedy.

The lyctid case that does occasionally happen here Correcting a misconception is not the same as saying the other insect never
appears, so here is the narrow situation in which a true powderpost beetle is
the right answer in this county.

What the insect looks like, and why you will probably never see one WSU describes the adults as reddish to chocolate brown and two to five
millimeters long — an eighth to a quarter of an inch on the PestSense sheet.
Cylindrical rather than flat, with the head tucked down under a hood-like
thorax, which is the giveaway when one turns up on a windowsill in July.

The moisture number, and why it is not the one on our termite page This is the fact that makes the beetle a Whatcom County problem rather than a
national one, and it is worth being precise because the figures published for
different organisms get blended together into a single vague warning about damp.

Why this county in particular Thirteen to eighteen percent is not an unusual condition here. It is the default
condition under a lot of the housing stock.

Frass, holes, and reading them properly Anobiid frass is the diagnostic feature, and the texture is the part people get
wrong.

Active or long finished — the only test that decides anything More money is wasted on this species than on any other in the library, and it is
wasted for one reason: holes are permanent and people read them as current.

Four to six years, and what that does to your expectations The larval stage is long. WSU puts it at four to five years feeding inside the
timber. The regional handbooks extend that to five or six years or longer in cool
damp wood, and cool damp wood is what we have.

The year, as it runs here The calendar for this species is short and it is worth knowing, because two of
the three useful things you can do are seasonal.
What to do before anybody comes out Four things, none of which cost anything.

Telling it from the wood-boring weevil These two are confused constantly, in both directions, and they are the two most
likely insects in a Whatcom County crawlspace to leave round holes and pale
powder.

What treatment involves, and what it depends on The verdict on this page is *depends*, and here is the honest account of what it
depends on.

What we will not do **Fumigate.** That is a response built for other species in other climates, and
proposing it for an anobiid in a Bellingham crawlspace is a sign the diagnosis
came from a national script.
What you get in writing Worth stating plainly, because this is the point where the industry gets vague.
How worried to be Less than the marketing suggests and more than the silence suggests.

Related work The service page covering this insect alongside the others that leave holes in
timber is
[wood-boring bee and beetle control](/services/carpenter-bee-control/), and the
broader structural picture sits on
[termite and wood-destroying pest control](/services/termite-control/). Because
the finding is nearly always a crawlspace finding,
[crawlspace cleanout and restoration](/services/craw

title: Aphaenogaster: The Ant With No Common Name
sections:
The ant nobody has a name for Most of the ants in this library arrive with a name attached. Carpenter ant.
Pavement ant. Odorous house ant. The name usually tells you the important thing
about the animal.

Recognizing them **Size.** Four to six millimeters, monomorphic — every worker the same. That
puts them squarely between the small indoor ants and the large carpenter and
thatching ants.
Why finding them is a moisture report This is the part worth carrying away from the page.

What they eat Seeds, dead and live insects, and other arthropods — so a predator and a
scavenger rather than a specialist.
Colony structure Colonies run to as many as three thousand workers with several queens.

The swarm, which is when people notice Reproductives swarm from late summer into fall, and that is when this species
generates calls.
The weak sting, and the honest scale of it The guidance handles this well and it is worth reproducing the sense of it.

Telling them from the ones that matter **Carpenter ant.** Larger and polymorphic — a range of worker sizes in one
colony — evenly rounded thoracic profile with no spines, usually black, and
genuinely excavating sound wood. This is the important distinction, because it
is the difference between an ant exploiting decay and an ant creating a
structural problem.

Around this county Ordinary and largely unremarked. They are part of the general ant fauna in soil,
under stones and boards, and in the decaying wood that a wet county produces in
quantity.

What we would actually do **Identify it**, because the spines make this quick and because the alternative
answers — carpenter ant in particular — are much more expensive to be wrong
about.
What we will not sell you We will not treat an ant colony in a stump in somebody's back garden.

The spines, and the other ant that has them Since the spines are the identifying feature, it is worth being precise about
the one genuine point of confusion.

Seeds, and where the name winnow ant comes from The seed handling is worth a paragraph because it is where one of the two
competing common names originates and because it explains something about where
these ants live.

Where we actually find them In practice, on jobs in this county, this genus turns up in a short list of
places and almost all of them are outdoors.

Why we would rather you called about the wood Somebody finding this ant in a building has, without knowing it, done a useful
piece of building inspection.

What this genus contributes to the library A page about an ant that rarely causes trouble might look like completeness for
its own sake, and it earns its place for a different reason.

The short version Four to six millimeters, brown to reddish-brown, all one size, with a pair of
spines on the back of the thorax. Nests in decaying wood, in existing cavities,
and in soil under stones and boards.

A note on the swarm, and what to check Since the swarm is the one time this genus is conspicuous, it is worth knowing
what to look at while it is happening, because the answer is time-limited.

title: Bald-Faced Hornet: Not Actually a Hornet
sections:
The name is wrong, and the mistake is expensive Almost everything people believe about this insect follows from a word that does
not apply to it.

What it looks like Bigger than anything else in the family here, and the color is the giveaway
before the size is.

The nest, which is the thing people actually see Very few households ever identify the insect. They identify the structure, and
it is the most recognizable object in this whole subject.
The number that surprises everybody Here is where the hornet framing does the most damage.
What it does with its summer, and where it does not go This is the most useful thing on the page and it is almost never said.
Defensiveness, in proportion The reputation is earned close in and unearned everywhere else.

The nest hanging in a bare tree in December This is where a pest control company either tells you the truth or takes your
money, so here it is plainly.

The April version of the same nest Everything on this page describes an August problem, and there is a version of
it in April that almost nobody acts on because almost nobody looks.

Aerial yellowjacket, and why the nest will not tell you The one species this gets genuinely confused with is its close relative, and the
confusion runs in a direction people do not expect.

Where the nest sits is what decides the job Species is not the variable that matters. Position is, and it sorts these nests
into four practical categories.

When we would leave it, and when we would not The case for leaving it: a nest away from paths, doors, seating, play areas and
anything anybody has to maintain; nobody in the household reacting badly to
stings; a colony that has already spent the summer removing insects from the
property without a single incident; and a date past the middle of September,
when the whole thing has weeks left regardle

What the work involves Where a nest does need dealing with, the shape of it is set by the fact that the
target is enclosed and elevated.

Around the county **Sudden Valley, Geneva and the Lake Whatcom margins.** Mature trees, dense
understory and a lot of properties where the boundary between garden and
woodland is a suggestion. Most of the high-in-a-tree nests we are asked about
are here, and most of them get left alone.

Related work The county-wide picture and the rest of the season sit on
[wasp and hornet control](/services/wasp-control/), and the specific case of a
big paper nest in a tree gets its own detailed treatment on
[bald-faced hornet nest in a tree](/services/wasp-control/bald-faced-hornet-nest-in-a-tree/).
If the wasps bothering you are at ground level rather than overhead, that is
[yellowjackets in t

title: Bed Bug (Cimex lectularius) in Whatcom County
sections:
The one thing to take from this page Bites do not confirm bed bugs. Nothing else on this page matters as much as that
sentence, and almost every expensive mistake made with this insect starts by
ignoring it.

They are not a cleanliness problem, and the shame is expensive [Washington's Department of Health](https://doh.wa.gov/community-and-environment/pests/bed-bugs) describes people bringing bed bugs into their
homes on infested luggage, furniture, bedding or clothing. That is the whole
mechanism. There is no dirt in it, no neglect, and no correlation with how a
household is kept.

What the insect actually looks like The University of Kentucky puts an adult at about three-sixteenths of an inch,
reddish-brown, with an oval flattened body — apple-seed coloring on something
closer to a lentil in size. The Pacific Northwest handbook describes them as
roughly half the size of a pencil eraser, which is the more useful comparison for
somebody holding one on a piece of tape.

Fecal spotting, cast skins, eggs, insects These are the four findings that establish an infestation, and they are worth
knowing individually because they appear at different stages and in different
places.

Where they actually are in a room Bed bugs stay close to a sleeping person. That is the single most useful
organizing fact about searching for them, and it is why an infestation in a
detached house is usually a bedroom problem rather than a house problem.

How they get from one place to another They are carried. Bed bugs do not come in from the yard, they are not drawn by
food waste, and they do not arrive on the wind.

Bed bug or carpet beetle This is the confusion that costs the most money in both directions, and it is
worth separating carefully.

What they do to people, and what they do not Washington's Department of Health is direct: there are no known cases of
infectious disease spread by bed bug bites. That is not a hedge, and it is
genuinely reassuring in a way the internet is reluctant to be.

Heat, cold and the numbers behind them The domestic tools that work on this insect work because of temperature, and the
figures are worth having.

Preparing for treatment, which is most of the outcome This is the part households are least warned about and the part that most often
decides whether a job holds.

What the work involves Treatment is aimed at harborage rather than sprayed across surfaces, because that
is where the insect spends its life. Seams, joints, voids, frame hardware, the
underside of furniture, the edges of the room and the penetrations that connect
one room to the next.

Monitoring, and what a clear result actually means Between a suspicion and a certainty there is a gap that a household can close
cheaply, and it is worth knowing what is in it.

Shared walls change the scope In a duplex, an apartment or a subdivided old house, the extent of the problem is
a property question rather than a tenancy question, and the arithmetic is
unforgiving.

What it costs, and why we verify first Bed bugs are the one service here that begins with a paid visit rather than a
free one, and the figures live on the
[bed bug control](/services/bed-bug-control/) page rather than on this one, where
they would drift out of date.

When it is not a bed bug If the marks are around ankles and calves and the insect jumps, look at the
[cat flea](/pest-library/cat-flea/) instead, and start by asking what animal has
been living in or under the building.

Where to start Tell us what you have found, where, and what changed in the weeks before it
started — travel, a piece of furniture, a guest, a move. Photograph anything you
find and keep a specimen on clear tape if you can, because a physical sample
settles in seconds what a description takes twenty minutes to circle around.

title: Boxelder Bug — The Red-and-Black Cluster on a Wall
sections:
The wall that turns red and black Somewhere in early October a Whatcom County homeowner walks around the corner of
their house and finds a couple of hundred insects packed onto the siding in the
afternoon sun. Flat, dark, half an inch long, marked with sharp red lines, sitting
shoulder to shoulder and not doing anything in particular.

Which boxelder bug Worth a paragraph, because most of the boxelder bug writing online describes a
different animal from the one on your siding.

Recognizing one **The adult** is about half an inch long, flat and elongated. The wings and thorax
are dark gray to black, overlaid with thin bright red or orange lines: a set
running lengthwise on the plate behind the head, a line down each side, and a
diagonal on each wing. Folded at rest, those lines resolve into a rough X or a
narrow triangle, depending on how the wings have settled.

What it is not Three insects arrive on the same walls in the same fortnight here, and boxelder
bugs are the easiest of the three to place.

The trees, and how far they travel These insects live on maples. The primary host is boxelder itself, *Acer negundo*,
with other maple species and ash as regular alternates. The handbook notes that in
high-population years they will also feed on developing fruit — apple, cherry,
peach, pear, plum — and its pear entry files the species as a minor orchard pest
where boxelder or maple stand nearby, p
The year they have One generation, or possibly two, and the sources are not unanimous.

Why they choose your wall The mechanism is heat, and it is the same for every overwintering insect in this
library.
What they do indoors, which is nothing Set this out plainly, because the fear is usually larger than the fact.
Vacuum, do not crush The correct tool is a vacuum cleaner and the correct instinct is not to squash.

Why our verdict is that treating is rarely warranted The line at the top of this page says rarely worth treating, and it is not
modesty. It is what the regional handbook says.
The spring repeat In March or April they come back, and it looks like the treatment failed.

Around this county **Riparian ground and the river corridors.** Boxelder is a floodplain tree, and the
Nooksack corridor, the sloughs and the wet margins around Everson, Nooksack and
Deming carry the host in quantity. Properties on that ground see the heaviest
autumn numbers in the county.
Why it is always the same wall Two things fix the location, and neither of them is anything you have done.
Children, pets and the things people worry about The questions arrive in a fairly fixed order and they all have short answers.

When it is worth a phone call anyway Given everything above, there are still three situations where we would rather
hear from you.

What is not worth your money **A fogger.** It does not reach a wall void, which is where they are, and it puts
product through the rooms, which is where they mostly are not.

The short version Black with red lines, in a crowd, on the sunny wall, in October. Harmless. Not
breeding indoors, not eating anything, not damaging the structure, effectively not
biting. They stain, so use a vacuum rather than your hand.

title: Brown Marmorated Stink Bug in Whatcom County
sections:
The insect on the windowsill in February A shield-shaped brown insect appears on the inside of an upstairs window in the
middle of winter. Nothing has been open for months, there is no obvious way in,
and the natural conclusion is that something is breeding in the house.

What it looks like WSU Tree Fruit describes *Halyomorpha halys* as one of the larger stink bugs in
Washington at 12 to 17 millimeters, marbled gray-brown, and shaped like the
heraldic shield that gives the whole family its shape.

What it is not Three insects generate the same photograph in our inbox each October, and the WSU
publication FS079E separates them explicitly.

Where it came from and where it is now The species reached the eastern United States around the mid-1990s, turning up in
Pennsylvania in 1996, and arrived in the Pacific Northwest in the mid-2000s with a
Portland detection. Washington's first documented sightings came in the fall of
2010, and at the time FS079E was published they were confined to Clark and
Skamania Counties in the far southwest of
Why it comes indoors The behavior is an overwintering strategy and nothing more.

The smell, and one correction They are called stink bugs for a reason. Disturbed, handled or crushed, they
release a defensive secretion described variously as coriander, burnt rubber or
something acrid, and it lingers in a room and in a vacuum canister.

The part that genuinely matters Everything above is a nuisance. The reason this species has a research program
behind it, a state distribution map and a public reporting address is agricultural.

Please report it This is the one species in our library where an ordinary sighting has value to
somebody.

What we do, and what we will not The verdict at the top of this page says it depends, and it depends on two things:
the month, and whether the building is a house or a growing operation.

Sealing, which is the half that lasts The openings that matter on a Whatcom County house are mostly at height, which is
why this problem survives on buildings where somebody has carefully sealed
everything they could reach from the ground.

Around this county **The agricultural corridor** — Lynden, Everson, Nooksack, Sumas. Properties beside
berry fields, orchards and large gardens see the highest autumn numbers, because a
population that built up over the growing season is looking for shelter and yours
is the nearest building.

A year in the life Knowing the whole cycle makes the indoor phase far less mysterious, and it takes a
paragraph each.

Why your building and not the neighbor's Households take this personally, and the profile of an affected building is
specific enough to be worth setting out.

If you rent These calls reach us from tenants at least as often as from owners, and the answer
is structural in both directions.

The short version It got in last October. It is not eating anything, not breeding, and not damaging
your house. It cannot bite you. Crushing it does not call in reinforcements, but
it does smell, so use a vacuum.

title: Bumble Bees: We Do Not Treat Them
sections: The position, stated first We do not treat bumble bees.

The trouble part, because it is the part people do not know Washington has at least 23 species of bumble bee, which is a larger number than
most people expect and a genuinely good thing for a state whose agriculture
leans on pollination.

The colony is annual, and that decides most cases This single fact resolves the great majority of bumble bee calls, and it is
different in kind from what a honey bee or a yellowjacket does.

Recognizing one The identification matters more than it looks, because the three things people
call bumble bees have three different answers.
Buzz pollination, and why the species matter here Worth a paragraph because it explains why an agricultural county cares.

Where the nests are, and what they look like Bumble bees do not excavate. They find a ready-made cavity with soft material in
it and move in, which is why the sites are so consistently domestic.

The insulation case, which is the one that worries people Of all the nest sites on that list, the one that produces the most anxious phone
calls is a colony in the insulation of a wall, a crawlspace, a garage ceiling or
an unfinished attic. It feels like the honey bee scenario, and it is not.

Temperament, and stings Bumble bees have a bad reputation they mostly do not earn, and one genuine
capability worth knowing.

The honest version of relocation People ask, and the answer they want is that we will scoop the nest into a box
and put it in a hedgerow.

When it genuinely cannot stay There are real cases, and pretending otherwise would make the rest of this page
less credible.

What we will actually do on a bumble bee call **Identify it, at no charge.** A photograph settles it in under a minute, and a
large share of these calls end there. The single most common outcome is that it
turns out to be a western yellowjacket in the ground, which is a wasp, is a
different animal in every respect, and is something we do treat.

Around this county **The agricultural corridor** — Lynden, Everson, Nooksack, Sumas. Berry and tree
fruit production here depends on pollination, wild bumble bees are part of that
workforce, and a nest in a field margin or a hedgerow is doing paid work nobody
is paying for.
Pesticide practice, since it is relevant here One thing worth stating because it applies well beyond this page.

The short version A bumble bee colony is small, gentle, temporary, and made up of an animal that
several state and university programs are actively trying to keep from
disappearing. It will be over by autumn. The nest will never be used again.
There is no honey to rot in your wall and no population to come back.

Related work The other bee we will not treat, and the reasons a colony in a wall is a
building problem, are on [honey bee](/pest-library/honey-bee/). Our overall
position on bees, including mason and mining bees, is on
[bee removal](/services/bee-removal/). A large bee and a round hole in bare wood
is [carpenter bee](/pest-library/carpenter-bee/) territory. And if the insect at
your table is smoot

title: Carpenter Ants in Whatcom County, WA
sections:
What you are actually holding Size settles most of these before anything else does. The WSU Clark County
Master Gardener sheet puts western carpenter ant workers between a quarter and
a half inch, with queens reaching three quarters of an inch, and describes them
as black except for reddish legs. Get one onto a sheet of white paper under a
lamp and the legs read reddish-brown rather than dark, whi

They excavate wood. They do not eat any of it. This is the single fact that explains everything else on this page, and it is
the one most consistently gotten wrong.

Frass, and what it is telling you The heap of coarse material below a gallery opening is the outdoor half of the
same fact. It is not sawdust in the sense of something a saw made — it is
excavated wood fiber that has been carried out deliberately, mixed with whatever
else the colony was clearing: shed wings from last spring's reproductives, legs
and head capsules from dead nestmates, the remains o

The spring swarmer problem Every April this county produces a run of calls that begin "I think I have
termites," and in the overwhelming majority of them the specimen on the
windowsill is a winged carpenter ant. This is the most common misidentification
in the region and it is worth taking apart properly, because the two answers
carry very different consequences and the wrong one gets treated for

Why swarmers indoors are the strongest signal on the page A colony does not produce reproductives until it can afford to. Penn State puts a
mature colony at roughly two to three thousand workers, reached over several
years, and only then does it begin turning out winged forms — somewhere around
two to four hundred a year.

Parent colonies, satellites, and why indoor-only treatment fails A carpenter ant population is not a nest. It is a network, and understanding the
shape of it is what separates work that holds from work that does not.
The hundred-yard radius The parent colony is often not on your property.

Where they turn up in this county's housing The pattern here is set by the wet season rather than by winter cold, and it
concentrates in a short list of places.
What the damage actually amounts to Proportion matters here, in both directions.

Telling them apart from the ants they get confused with **Moisture ants** are the confusion that most often runs the other way — small
yellowish ants in a wet sill get reported as carpenter ants because the location
fits. Size resolves it immediately, since WSU puts moisture ant workers at three
to five millimeters against a carpenter ant's quarter inch and up, and color
resolves it again, yellow

Why this one is worth treating, and what that involves Carpenter ants get a treat verdict for reasons that do not apply to most of this
library. The colony does not run its course seasonally. It does not leave when
the weather changes. It expands into a building on its own schedule, it operates
mostly at night in places nobody looks, and left alone it compounds a decay
problem that is already runn

What makes it worse Spraying the trail, which removes the diagnostic route and leaves the network
intact. Sealing the gallery opening the frass is coming out of, which hides the
best marker on the building without closing anything. Retail bait stations
formulated only for sugar-feeders, which a colony provisioning for brood will
walk past. Sweeping up the frass before anyone has seen it. And treat

title: Carpenter Bees in Whatcom County: Usually Not
sections:
Start with the likely answer If you are reading this because a large dark bee is working around your deck,
your eaves or your fence in Whatcom County, the probability sits heavily on one
side: it is a bumble bee.

The one difference that settles it Ignore size. Both are large, both are dark, both are loud in flight, and neither
comparison works without the other insect present.
If it is a bumble bee Then the answer is to leave it, and that is the whole answer.
What an actual carpenter bee hole looks like Now the minority case.
The wood they choose, and the wood they ignore Bare and weathered softwood, on horizontal or downward-facing surfaces.
The male that charges you Worth its own heading because it drives more phone calls than the damage does.
They are pollinators, and that is load-bearing This matters to the verdict, so it is not a courtesy paragraph.
When the damage is cosmetic, and when it stops being Both halves of this are true and the industry usually only tells you one.

The year, as it runs here Both insects on this page are seasonal, and a lot of unnecessary work gets booked
because somebody called at the wrong point in the cycle.
Why so much of the advice you will find is wrong for here Worth naming, because it is the reason this page exists at all.

What to send before anybody drives out Identification does almost all of the work on this species, and it can be done
from a phone.
Woodpeckers, which do the visible damage The most dramatic damage attributed to carpenter bees is usually not theirs.
What we would actually do The verdict on this page is *rarely warranted*, and it is honest.

What we will not sell you **A recurring plan for a bee that is uncommon here.** The genus is not abundant
in this county, the damage is slow, and an annual subscription against it is not
a defensible product.

Related work The service page pairing this insect with the beetles that leave holes in timber
is [wood-boring bee and beetle control](/services/carpenter-bee-control/). If the
large bee turns out to be a honey bee swarm or a colony in a wall, that is
[bee removal](/services/bee-removal/), and the answer there also usually starts
with leaving them alone. Where the insect in your eaves is a wasp or

title: Carpet Beetle (Anthrenus spp.) — Larvae, Not Adults
sections:
You are looking at the wrong life stage Nearly every carpet beetle call starts with beetles on a windowsill, and nearly
every one of those beetles is harmless.

It came in with something, or it was already here Before any of the searching, it is worth settling where this problem comes from,
because the answer changes what money is worth spending.
What the adults and larvae actually look like Worth separating properly, because they look like two unrelated animals.
The cast skins are the evidence If you remember one search instruction from this profile, make it this one.

Keratin, and the soiling exception The diet is the same protein the clothes moth is after, and the list is short
enough to memorize.

The rash that gets read as bites This is why the [bed bug](/pest-library/bed-bug/) profile sends people here, and
it deserves careful handling rather than a confident one.

The source nobody thinks of When there is a beetle problem and no wool anywhere, the answer is almost always
something dead.
When they show up here Development is slow, and our climate makes it slower.

Carpet beetle or clothes moth They eat the same protein and damage the same items, so the separation is done on
leftovers.

The cleaning that does most of the work For a straightforward fabric case, the household does more than any application
does, and it is worth being specific about the order.
When treatment is warranted, and when it is not The verdict here is *depends*, and it splits cleanly in two.

Where they turn up around the county The pattern here follows housing stock and bird habit more than it follows any
map of climate.

What we will not do **Broadcast product across the floor of a room people live in.** Application
belongs in harborage, and a treated floor does not reach a larva under a rug edge
anyway.

Where to start Collect a specimen if you can. A larva or a cast skin on clear tape, or a sharp
photograph next to a fingertip for scale, settles the identification faster than
any description.

title: Cat Flea (Ctenocephalides felis) in Whatcom County
sections:
The dog flea that is not Somebody in Whatcom County finds fleas on a dog and reasonably calls them dog
fleas. The species is almost certainly *Ctenocephalides felis*, the cat flea,
and the name is a historical accident rather than a description of its habits.

The fact that explains almost everything else Here is the number to carry: about ninety-five percent of the fleas in an
infested house are not fleas you can see.

The life cycle, stage by stage **Eggs.** A female cat flea produces about twenty to fifty of them a day, per UC
IPM — Missouri extension puts a lifetime figure at up to eight hundred. They are
pearly white, oval and about a thirty-second of an inch, and crucially they are
not sticky. They fall off the animal within hours of being laid, wherever it
happens to be standing. That single detail redirec

Why fleas appear in an empty house This is the single most misread situation in the whole subject, and once the
pupal stage is understood it stops being mysterious.

Confirming it is a flea at all Two other things get reported as fleas here often enough that it is worth being
able to rule them out from an armchair.

When this does not need us The library is meant to say so where that is the truth, and with fleas there is a
real case for it.

Where the source is when there is no pet A flea problem in a house with no animal in it is not really a flea problem. It is
an animal problem with fleas attached, and treating the carpet without resolving
the source buys a few good weeks.
What goes on the animal is a veterinary decision We do not treat animals and we will not tell you what to put on one.

What the household half looks like The part homeowners control genuinely changes the result, which is not something
we say about most pests.

How the property gets treated **Confirm the insect first.** Springtails and carpet beetle larvae are the two
things most often reported as fleas in this county, and neither responds to any of
this. A flea is laterally flattened, dark, hard to crush, and jumps.

What fleas do to people and animals For most people, flea bites are itching and small red marks concentrated on the
ankles and lower legs. Purdue notes that several bites more or less in a row are
characteristic of one flea feeding repeatedly, which is the pattern that gets
mistaken for something worse.
The year here Our climate stretches the season at both ends rather than producing a sharp peak.

What does not work **Flea bombs and total-release foggers.** They deposit on the tops of things. The
larvae and pupae are down in the fiber and in the cracks, which the product does
not reach, and the pupal stage is untouched either way.

Where to start Tell us whether there is an animal in the house, whether it has been treated by a
vet, and whether anything has been living under the floor or in the roof. Those
three answers determine the whole shape of the visit.

title: Cellar Spider: The Real Daddy Longlegs Story
sections:
The spider in the corner, and the story attached to it There is a small-bodied spider on absurdly long thin legs hanging upside down in
the corner of your basement, your garage, your laundry room or the underside of
your deck. It has been there a while. The web around it has gone gray with dust.

Three unrelated animals, one nickname Before anything else, because almost every argument about this subject is two
people describing different creatures.

The venom claim, taken apart Here is the myth in its standard form: *daddy longlegs have the most toxic venom
of any spider in the world, but their fangs are too short to penetrate human
skin.*

What the television demonstration actually settled Somebody always raises it, so it is worth handling directly rather than
pretending it is not part of the conversation.

Recognizing one The shape is unmistakable once you have seen it, and it is nothing like the
other spiders that turn up indoors in this county.

Telling it from a giant house spider These two share basements and garages across this county and they get reported
to us in the same phone call, usually as "spiders in the crawlspace." They are
not remotely similar once you know what to look at, and the separation takes
about two seconds rather than a microscope.

The web, and why it is such a mess A cellar spider builds an irregular mesh of threads rather than a patterned
structure. There is no wheel, no funnel, no sheet — just a loose three-
dimensional tangle strung across a corner, under a joist, behind a water heater,
over a basement window or across the angle where a wall meets a ceiling.

It hunts other spiders This is the part that changes how the animal reads, and it comes straight from
the extension literature rather than from folklore.

Where they live in this county Cellar spiders are indoor animals here in a way that most spiders are not, and
the local building stock decides where they turn up.

The bite question, answered properly For completeness, because people ask, and because the honest answer differs from
the one the myth sets up.
What to actually do The honest version, in order of how much good it does.

Our verdict, and what sits behind it Rarely worth treating, and never worth treating for what the animal might do,
because it does not do anything.

If you want it identified Send a photograph. A shot from the side showing the body against the legs is
enough, and a coin or a fingertip in the frame settles the scale question that
long legs make so confusing.

Related work The other spider that shares a crawlspace with this one is the
[giant house spider](/pest-library/giant-house-spider/), which is larger, faster
and also harmless. Our general position on spiders, including why spraying does
less than people expect, is on
[spider control](/services/spider-control/). If the crawlspace under the house
is what is producing the insects that feed everything

title: Cluster Fly: The Slow One at the Winter Window
sections:
The fly nobody expects It is January. There is a slow, dark, slightly hairy fly bumping against the
inside of an upstairs window, and there are eleven more on the sill. Outside it
is 40 degrees and raining. Nothing has been left out, nothing has died, and
nobody can work out where they came from.

The earthworm, which is the whole explanation Almost everything counterintuitive about this insect follows from one fact about
its larvae.

A blow fly that is not a filth fly Worth a short section, because it is the one thing about the classification that
genuinely confuses people who look it up.

Recognizing one The identification is easy once you know what to look at, and it hinges on three
things.
The name, and why we list a genus Two small points about naming, both of which come up.
Why your building, and why the upstairs windows The autumn behavior is what turns a soil insect into a household one.

The same story as the stink bugs Cluster flies almost never arrive alone, and the reason is that they are one
member of a group of insects doing exactly the same thing on exactly the same
calendar.

What the flies are actually telling you Since the insect itself is telling you nothing about your housekeeping, it is
worth asking what it *is* telling you, because there is real information in it.

The dead flies, which is the part people skip A share of the overwintering population dies in the void, and in a building that
has had this for years the accumulation can be considerable.
Where this happens in Whatcom County The pattern here follows land use more than anything else.

The year, as it runs in this county Written out because the whole recommendation is a calendar, and because knowing
which month you are in tells you what is worth doing.

Our verdict, and what it turns on This one genuinely depends, and the variable is the calendar more than the
property.

What we will not sell you **A monthly plan through the winter.** The population inside the building is
fixed once they are in. Repeat visits do not reduce it and the calendar proves
it.

What to tell us if you call **Which windows.** Two or three specific ones almost always, and that narrows
the void they are in more than anything else you could say.

Related work The practical, building-by-building version of this is
[cluster flies in upstairs windows](/services/fly-control/cluster-flies-in-upstairs-windows/).
The species-by-species guide to every other fly, and why finding the source is
the whole job on all of them, is [fly control](/services/fly-control/). The
sealing itself is [exclusion and repairs](/services/exclusion-and-repairs/), and
t

title: Cross Orbweaver: The Big September Garden Web
sections:
The one you walked into Somewhere in the first half of September, in a great many Whatcom County
households, somebody walks out to the car in the dark and puts their face
through a web. Then they look up and find something the size of a grape hanging
in the middle of it, patterned, motionless, and apparently enormous.

Recognizing one The mark that gives the species its name is a set of pale spots on top of the
abdomen, arranged into a rough cross. Penn State Extension describes four
elongated spots toward the front of the abdomen forming the shape, on a
background that runs anywhere from yellow through brown to dark gray, with a
carapace carrying three darker lengthwise bands.

The web is the giveaway A cross orbweaver builds the textbook spider web: a vertical wheel with radiating
spokes and a spiral of sticky capture silk, up to about 40 centimeters across,
strung between whatever anchor points are available. Doorways, gaps between
shrubs, the space between a downspout and a railing, fence lines, the frame of a
window, the gap between a wing mirror and a hedge.

What the web actually costs the spider The scale of the thing is worth sitting with for a moment, because it explains
why removing one is such a mild act.

The web as a food-supply reading This is the practical part, and it applies to every spider on the property rather
than just this one.

Why September The season is a life-cycle effect rather than a weather effect, and it is the
same story that drives every spider question here in autumn.

It does not live in your house Worth stating clearly, because it is the fear behind most of the calls: this is
not a spider that moves indoors.

Bites, briefly Washington's NatureMapping fact sheet describes the bite as slightly unpleasant
and harmless to people. Utah State Extension records orb weavers as not known to
be a health hazard, and lists them as beneficial. Penn State's entry, which is
the most cautious of the three, notes that verified bites can produce pain,
swelling and redness, with occasional broader discomfort, and reactio

What to do about a web in the way A web across a doorway, a gate, a path or the space where you park is a genuine
nuisance and you are entitled to remove it. There is no conservation argument for
walking into silk twice a day.

Why our verdict is that we do not treat these The verdict at the top of this page says we do not treat for cross orbweavers.
That is a real position rather than a rhetorical one, and here is the reasoning
behind it.

The other big webs you will see here A few other web-builders turn up in Whatcom County gardens in the same weeks, and
knowing the differences saves a certain amount of alarm.

Where you meet them around this county The distribution around a property follows the food and the anchor points, and it
is fairly predictable once you know what to look for.
Names, and what people mistake it for The common names are a small mess and it causes some confusion.

Living with the September spider For most households the proportionate response to all of this is a broom, a
different porch light, and a slightly better September.

title: Deer Mouse (Peromyscus maniculatus) in Whatcom County
sections: An outdoor animal that lets itself in The most useful thing to understand about this species is where it belongs.

Deer mouse or house mouse This is the identification that changes the advice, and it is easy once you know
what to look at. Both UC IPM publications set out the same features.
The cache is a signature There is a fifth check that costs nothing and that almost nobody knows about.

Hantavirus, stated accurately This is the reason the deer mouse gets its own page rather than a paragraph on
another one, and it is the section where being precise matters most.

The cleanup method, in order This is Washington's own procedure, and it is the part of this page worth
printing out. It applies to any rodent waste, not just to what you think is a
deer mouse, for the simple reason given in the FAQ above.

Opening a building that has been shut Because this is the situation the guidance was written for, it is worth setting
out as a sequence rather than a principle. It applies to a cabin in April, a
shed you have not been into since autumn, a trailer coming out of storage, or a
crawlspace hatch nobody has lifted in three years.

Where they get in, and what they nest in Deer mice use the same openings every rodent uses, at the same quarter-inch
threshold set out on the [house mouse](/pest-library/house-mouse/) page and in
Whatcom County's own rodent guidance, which tells residents to seal holes and
gaps bigger than a quarter of an inch. UC IPM's exclusion advice for this
species is the same figure — seal openings larger th

The home range problem House mouse work is close-quarters work because the animal lives in a small
space. Deer mouse work is not, and this is where people go wrong with traps.

What they damage **Soft goods, comprehensively.** The list above, and it is the damage people
actually notice.

Trapping, and the two tools that are not available Trapping is the method, and the mechanics are close to house mouse work with two
differences.

Closing the building Everything above argues toward the same conclusion, which is that the durable
work on a deer mouse is physical rather than chemical.

The season, here Pressure follows the same curve as everything else in this county — rising from
late September, hard through October and November, elevated all winter. The
mechanism is the ordinary one: cover dies back, outdoor food declines, ground
saturates, and a dry closed building becomes the best thing available.

When it is not a deer mouse If the animal is uniformly gray-brown from shoulder to belly with a bare tail of
one color, it is a [house mouse](/pest-library/house-mouse/), and the work is
tighter, more indoors, and organized around a much smaller territory.

Where to start Tell us what you have found and where, leave a representative patch of evidence
undisturbed if you reasonably can, and do not start sweeping.

title: European Earwigs in Whatcom County
sections:
The pincers first, because nothing else gets read until they are dealt with Almost every call about this insect is really a call about the back end of it,
so we will settle that before anything else.

What the animal actually is **Size and color.** Adults run about five eighths of an inch by Penn State's
figure and up to three quarters by UC IPM's, dark reddish-brown, with a reddish
head and yellow-brown legs. The Pacific Northwest handbook gives about
five eighths of an inch, light to dark brown, with pale legs — which is the
description that matches what turns up here.
Why this county produces so many One generation a year, and the population is decided before anybody notices it.
The population is in the first three feet This is where the job is, and it is a narrow band.
They do not infest a structure Stated flatly, because it is the fact that decides the verdict.
Where they come in They are flat, they are small, and they are following dark and damp.

Outdoors they are mostly on your side This is the part of the page most likely to change what somebody does, so it is
worth the space.

Why the verdict is "rarely warranted" Because on most properties the honest work is an afternoon with a rake and a
door sweep, and that is what "rarely warranted" means on this site.

And what makes it warranted anyway Having spent this page recommending a rake, here is the other side, because
"rarely" is not "never".

Where they turn up hardest in this county The distribution follows landscaping and shade rather than housekeeping, which
is worth saying because these calls often arrive with an apology attached.

Telling it from what it is not Misidentification is less common here than with the spiders, but it happens in
three predictable directions.

What people have usually already tried Most households have done two or three things before they call, and it is worth
saying which of them were wasted effort.

What we will not do **Spray the inside of a house for an insect that is dying on the floor.** The
ones indoors have days at most. Product applied to interior baseboards changes
their outcome very little and the outdoor population not at all.

What to tell us if you do call **Which rooms.** Bathroom, laundry and kitchen means humidity and a threshold.
An upstairs bedroom is a different picture and worth mentioning.

title: European Paper Wasp: The One That Is Not a Yellowjacket
sections:
A wasp that was not here when most of this county was built There is a specific conversation we have with people who have lived in Whatcom
County for forty years, and it goes like this: there did not used to be this
many wasps under the eaves.

Why everybody calls it a yellowjacket Because at a glance it is a yellow and black wasp about half an inch long, and
in this county that description belongs to something else.

The open comb, which nothing else here makes A yellowjacket nest is a sealed object. Whether it is underground, inside a wall
or hanging in a shrub, the comb is wrapped in a paper envelope and all you ever
see from outside is a structure and an entrance hole.

Where it puts the comb, and why that is the whole problem If this wasp only built under eaves it would barely register as a pest. Its
actual site selection is what generates calls, because it favors small enclosed
cavities, and small enclosed cavities on a residential property are mostly
things people put their hands into.

Telling it from the paper wasp that was already here Washington had paper wasps before this one arrived, and the native is still
around, so the comb under your eave is not automatically the introduced species.

How defensive it actually is Considerably less than the insect it resembles, and being straight about this is
most of the value of the page.

The head start, and the one place the annual rule bends Every wasp colony in this county is annual. A queen that mated the previous
autumn starts alone in spring, the colony builds through summer, new queens and
males leave to mate, and the rest of it — workers, males, the founding queen —
does not survive the cold. Only mated queens carry over, sheltering somewhere
else entirely.
Why the identification changes the answer Here is the reason this profile exists.
What it does for you Not nothing, and it belongs on the ledger.

When it is genuinely worth dealing with The verdict at the top of this page is that treatment is rarely warranted, and
the exceptions are specific rather than vague.

What we would actually do For an accessible comb in a bad position, the work is small. The right hour is
early morning or after dusk, when the adults are on the nest and slow rather
than out foraging, and the comb comes off its stalk. Where there is no cavity
involved, that is frequently the whole job.

What we will not sell you **A perimeter spray for paper wasps.** They do not walk your siding; they fly to
a cavity. Wetting the wall does very little and it does it to a great many
insects that were not the point.

Around the county **Older Bellingham housing.** Porch rails, shakes, meter boxes and a century of
odd penetrations in the siding. The highest density of nests per property that
we see, and the highest proportion of them that can safely be ignored.

Related work The seasonal picture across all the stinging species sits on
[wasp and hornet control](/services/wasp-control/). If what you have is going
into a hole in a wall rather than sitting on an open comb, read
[wasp nest in a wall void](/services/wasp-control/wasp-nest-in-a-wall-void/)
before anybody seals anything. The species most often confused with this one is
the [western yellowjacket](

title: Winter Ants: The Ones Foraging in February
sections:
The ant that turns up before spring There is a call this company gets every year in late winter, and it surprises
people every time. Ants — a proper trail of them — running into a kitchen in
February or early March, when the weather is still miserable and nothing else is
moving.
The names, and what they mean This ant carries three common names and all of them appear in the literature.
Recognizing them **Size and color.** Two to four millimeters, yellow to brown, monomorphic.
Why the cold does not stop them The short answer is that they are adapted to it, and the strategy is a good one.

Where they nest, and why it is not your house They nest in **soil**, outdoors, and they may **trail into structures in
inclement weather**.

How they get in, and the fix that lasts The extension note is specific and it is the most useful sentence on this page
for a homeowner: **vegetation in contact with structures provides avenues to
enter**.
Why we rarely treat them Four reasons, and they compound.
What people usually do instead Two things, and both are worth heading off.

Around this county This is a genuinely common local call and it clusters in a way that fits
everything above.
What we would actually do **Confirm the species**, which at that time of year is usually quick.

What we will not sell you We will not sell a treatment program for an ant that is active for six weeks
and nests in somebody's lawn.

What else is moving in February Since the timing is the identifying feature of this ant, it is worth knowing what
else could be responsible for an insect indoors in late winter, because a couple
of them matter much more.

The honeydew connection Their food list includes honeydew, and that shapes where the outdoor trails run
in a way worth knowing if the indoor trail is being traced back.
Why the timing makes this ant easy to mis-sell There is a commercial hazard specific to this species and it is worth naming.

Around this county This is a common winter call across the older parts of Bellingham and in the
established neighborhoods of the towns, and the pattern is consistent enough to
predict.

What the season is actually telling you There is a wider point here that applies beyond this species, and it is the
reason this page exists rather than a line on the odorous house ant entry.

The trail you can follow yourself Because the nest is outdoors and the ants are large enough to see, this is one of
the few species on this site where a householder can realistically do the
diagnostic work themselves.

What to do if you would rather not wait for March If the trail is active now and you want it stopped today rather than after the
next dry weekend, a bait placed directly on the line will do it. They take sweet
baits readily, which is one of the few things about this ant that is
straightforward.

title: Ghost Ants: Rare Here, and Usually Something Else
sections:
The honest answer first The ghost ant is a real insect and it is a genuine structural pest. It is also
tropical, it is not established outdoors anywhere in the Pacific Northwest, and
the regional extension guide to the key ant pests of Washington, Oregon and
Idaho does not include it.
What a ghost ant actually looks like The name is a good description, which is not always true of common names.

What you probably have instead Four ants get reported in the same words — small, pale, indoors, in a trail —
and all four are more likely here than a ghost ant.
The test that settles most of these Crush one and smell it.

Why the identification matters more here than usual For most ants, getting the species slightly wrong costs you some efficiency.
With this group it can cost you the job, because of one behavior.
If it really is a ghost ant The situation would look like this.

Why we would not simply treat and move on Because a tropical tramp ant established in a heated building in Whatcom County
would be a genuinely unusual finding, and unusual findings are worth confirming
rather than assuming.

What this page is really for Most people who arrive here will have searched "tiny ants in the house" and
landed on the most exotic-sounding answer, which is a normal thing for a search
engine to do and a bad basis for a treatment.

Sending us something to identify We will identify a specimen for nothing, and we would rather do that than quote
for a treatment aimed at the wrong insect.

What we will not sell you We will not tell you that you have ghost ants because it sounds more serious
than odorous house ants. That would be a straightforward lie for money, and this
species is exactly the kind of exotic-sounding name that could be used that way.

What a tramp ant is, and why it matters Ghost ants belong to a small group of species that entomologists call **tramp
ants**, and the label explains almost everything about how they behave in
buildings.
Why the climate stops them outdoors here Ghost ants are a tropical species and their limit is cold, not competition.
Greenhouses, nurseries and anybody receiving plants If ghost ants are going to appear in this county, this is where.
If we found them, what the work would look like Bait first and bait only, at least to begin with.
What would make us change our minds about this page We would rather write this down than quietly revise it later.

Why a specimen beats a description Everything on this page turns on identification, so it is worth saying how ants
are actually identified rather than leaving it as something that happens
elsewhere.

title: Giant House Spider: Big, Fast, and Harmless
sections:
What you are looking at If you are reading this in September with a large brown spider in front of you,
this is almost certainly the animal. The giant house spider produces more alarmed
phone calls in Whatcom County than every other arthropod combined, and it is
harmless.

Where it lives This is a western Washington animal specifically. WSU records it as common in
Washington homes west of the Cascade Mountains, along with the coastal regions of
Oregon and British Columbia, and absent from the country east of the Cascades.
Whatcom County sits comfortably inside that range.
