The web, and where the spider sits It is a funnel weaver. The web is a flat, roughly horizontal sheet of silk with a
tube at one edge where the spider waits. Insects that blunder onto the sheet get
tangled long enough for a very fast animal to cross it and take them.

Why they appear all at once in autumn WSU puts peak visibility at mid-summer to early fall, when males in particular
are highly mobile. That is the mechanism, and it is worth stating precisely
because nearly every intuitive explanation for it is wrong.

More spiders means more insects The single most useful thing to understand about spider numbers is that they are
downstream of something else.

What it eats, and what it competes with A giant house spider takes whatever walks or blunders onto its sheet: flies,
small moths, beetles, ants, sowbugs, silverfish, midges, and a steady stream of
the smaller arthropods that live in a damp Pacific Northwest crawlspace. In a
garage or an outbuilding this adds up to real volume across a season.

Egg sacs and the quiet part of the year The season most people never think about is the one where intervention is
cheapest.

Telling it from a hobo spider This is the question the page exists to answer honestly, and the honest answer is
uncomfortable.
Why the identification matters less than it feels like it should Here is the part that a fear-based version of this page could never print.

What a bite would be, if you managed one People ask, so: WSU's position is that the bite of this species is not known to
pose any threat to humans, and that is the whole medical entry.
The one in the bathtub Practically, the most common encounter in this county.
What it means for a Whatcom County house Local housing stock shapes this more than the species does.
Our verdict, and why Rarely worth treating. Not never — but rarely, and not because of the species.

Send us a photograph Identification costs nothing and it settles most questions in a couple of
minutes. Photograph from directly above with a coin or a fingertip in the frame,
and from the side if you can. If the spider is in a clear container, a shot
through the base showing the underside is the single most useful angle, because
that is where the sternum is.

title: Grass-Carrying Wasp: The Grass in Your Window Track
sections:
What you are actually looking at Somebody opens a sliding window in late summer and finds the channel packed
with dry grass, cut to length and stuffed in tight. Sometimes there is a
green cricket in there too, not moving. It looks like something went badly
wrong in the window frame.

The nest, and why the window Grass-carrying wasps do not excavate. They take over a cavity that already
exists — a hollow plant stem, an old beetle tunnel, a nail hole, a weep hole,
a gap beneath siding, and very often the track of a sliding window or door.
Extension guidance from [Ohio State](https://bygl.osu.edu/node/2676) names window wells, weep holes and gaps
beneath siding in the same list,

She is not defending anything This is the part worth saying plainly, because the shape of a large
thread-waisted wasp near a window sets off the same alarm a yellowjacket does,
and the two could hardly be less alike in temperament.

Why we usually tell you to leave it Ohio State's guidance says management is not required, and that the contents
of a window well can be cleared if they are unsightly or interfere with
opening a window. That is our answer too, and it is the honest one: this is a
cleaning job and, if you want it not to recur, a sealing job.

Recognizing her She is a thread-waisted wasp: a long, narrow body with a conspicuously slender
stalk between thorax and abdomen, black or very dark, sometimes with a faint
sheen on the wings, and around three quarters of an inch to an inch long. The
waist is the giveaway. Yellowjackets and paper wasps are comparatively thick
through the middle; this one looks as though it were assembled from two p

What she is not Four insects get confused with this one, and separating them matters because
the correct response to each is different.

What she hunts Tree crickets and young katydids, which explains where she came from and why
she turned up when she did.
The year, in this county She is a summer insect here and the sequence is consistent.

Where the cavities are on a real house She does not excavate. Everything she uses was already there, and the full list
is worth knowing because closing them is the entire preventive measure.
Weep holes deserve their own paragraph Because the wrong fix here causes an actual building problem.
What happens if you do nothing Nothing dramatic, which is the honest answer.

Timing, if you would rather clear it If the reason for clearing is a window that will not shut, clear it whenever you
need to. It is a minute with a vacuum or a flat blade.

What not to do **Do not spray the track.** A residual insecticide in a window channel puts
product at hand height on a surface people touch, to no purpose — the occupant
is either sealed in a cell the spray will not reach or already gone.
What the nest actually tells you about your building This is worth more than the wasp is.

Solitary and social, and why the distinction runs through everything Nearly every wasp question we are asked comes down to this one fact, and almost
nobody has been told it.

What a visit for this looks like We identify what is actually in the cavity first, because grass, mud and paper
mean three different things and we are not going to guess from a photograph
when we could be standing in front of it.

What we will not sell you We will not sell a treatment program for a solitary wasp with no colony to
suppress and no habit of defending anything.

If you have an insect hotel A fair number of these calls come from people who deliberately put up a bee
hotel and then found something unexpected using it.

One thing worth checking while you are there If she used a window track, look at the other tracks on the same elevation
before you put the vacuum away. Sliding windows tend to be installed in runs,
they share a detail, and a female that found one suitable channel will very
often have used two or three. Clearing them all in one go takes another few
minutes and saves finding the next one in November

title: Great Golden Digger Wasp: Big, Orange, and Harmless
sections:
What it looks like, and why it worries people Big. That is the first thing. A great golden digger wasp is large enough to
carry a katydid, which means she is large enough to make anybody step back
when she lands on a driveway.

She is solitary, and that is the whole safety answer Every genuinely dangerous stinging insect on this site is social. A
yellowjacket or a bald-faced hornet has a colony, workers whose job includes
defense, and a nest worth dying for. That is what makes an accidental approach
expensive.

The burrow and the soil She digs a vertical tunnel with cells at the bottom, and where she digs it is
particular. The nesting research on this species is about site selection:
well-drained soil of moderate compactness, avoiding substrate loose enough to
collapse and ground packed too hard to work. In practice that means sandy or
sandy-loam ground, warm, with sparse vegetation.

Why we will not treat it Because there is nothing to treat. She is a solitary predator of katydids and
crickets, she visits flowers as an adult, she will not defend a nest, and the
season is short. A pesticide application here would be sold on the strength of
her size and nothing else.

The katydid, and what paralyzed means The footage above shows the part people find hardest to believe. She is
dragging a katydid several times her own bulk across open gravel, and the
katydid is not dead.

Watching one work If you find her, the sequence is worth two minutes of anybody's time, and it is
entirely safe to stand and watch.

The burrow, and what it looks like from above A neat round hole, roughly pencil to finger width, in bare or thinly vegetated
ground, often with a small fan of excavated soil beside it. The tunnel runs down
several inches and branches into cells at the bottom.

The one confusion that actually matters There is a ground-nesting wasp in this county that is genuinely dangerous, and
telling it apart from this one is the most useful thing on this page.

Where she nests, and why that is usually the whole problem The soil requirement is strict enough that her burrow is nearly always in one of
a few places: a gravel drive edge, a sandy bank, a path, a dry sunny border with
thin cover, the bare strip beside a shed or a slab.
Adults eat nectar Worth saying, because it changes how people think about her.

The season here Short. Adults are on the wing in the warm part of summer, roughly July into
early September in this county, with the peak of provisioning in the hottest,
driest weeks.

What not to do **Do not pour anything down the burrow.** Gasoline, diesel, bleach and boiling
water all circulate as folk remedies for ground-nesting insects. Fuel poured into
soil is a genuine contamination problem, it is unlawful to use a product in a
way inconsistent with its labeling, and none of it is necessary here.

When we would actually do something There is a version of this that warrants intervention and we would rather name
it than pretend there is none.

What a visit for this looks like We identify the insect first, and on a ground nest that is the whole job in most
cases: confirm it is a solitary digger and not a yellowjacket colony, which is a
two-minute observation and the difference between "leave it" and "this needs
handling today".

What we will not sell you We will not treat a solitary ground-nesting wasp because a customer found it
alarming. If we did that we would be charging for the size of an insect.

The other solitary ground-nesters here She is not the only insect that puts holes in bare ground, and the others get
reported to us under the same description. Sorting them is quick.

Photographing one for identification Since the entire practical question is "is this the harmless one or the
dangerous one", and since nobody should be approaching a hole to find out, a
photograph is usually the right first move.

What to tell whoever mows The single most useful thing anybody can do about ground-nesting insects is
tell the person operating the machinery where the holes are.

If she nests in the same place next year She may, because the ground is what she chose it for, and a returning female is
a sign the soil suits rather than a sign of an escalating problem. There is no
accumulating nest and no growing colony. Each season is a fresh female doing the
same short piece of work, and a burrow that reappears in the same bank three
summers running is three separate insects

title: Harvester Ants: A Real Sting, Mostly East of Here
sections:
Written for the trip rather than the house This is the one page in this library that is not really about Whatcom County,
and it is more useful for being honest about that.

Recognizing them **Size.** Six to eight millimeters, monomorphic. Large, and all one size — no
mix of big and small workers in a trail.
The nest, and what it looks like from a distance The nest gives itself away long before the ants do.

The sting This is the reason the species matters at all, and it is worth stating without
either exaggerating or downplaying it.

Where people actually get stung The guidance is unusually specific and it is worth quoting in substance: people
who are stung are usually engaged in picnicking, fishing, rockhounding or other
recreational activities.

Seeds, and why they are called harvesters They collect seeds — mostly of grasses and various weeds — carry them
underground, and store them.

Where they are a genuine agricultural problem One specific case, and it is a good example of a pest being a pest only in
context.

What you probably have instead, here Somebody in Whatcom County looking at a large reddish ant is much more likely
looking at one of these.

If you genuinely have them here It is not impossible — the guidance says various species occur throughout the
Pacific Northwest even though the concentration is eastern — and the response
would depend entirely on where the nest is.

What we will not sell you We will not treat a large ant because it is large. That is the same principle
this library applies to the great golden digger wasp, and it holds here: size is
not a hazard signal, and the ants in this region that genuinely warrant caution
are identified by what they are rather than how big they look.

Why it is in a Pacific Northwest key at all Somebody reading this page in Bellingham might reasonably ask why a mostly
eastern-Washington ant sits in a publication about the whole region, and the
answer is instructive about how these guides are built.

The sting compared with what people know Since the guidance compares it to a honey bee or yellowjacket sting, the
comparison is worth extending, because most people calibrate insect risk from
those two.

What to do if you are stung Since the guidance compares it to a bee or wasp sting, the response is the same
as for those, and it is worth setting out plainly for somebody who has just had
one on a river bar with no phone signal.

For anybody working out there Field crews, surveyors, utility workers, agricultural staff and anybody else
spending working days on dry open ground in eastern Washington have a slightly
different exposure from a family on a picnic.

The identification service, applied to this one Since almost every report of this species in Whatcom County turns out to be
something else, this is one of the pages where the free identification does the
most work.

The short version Large, reddish, all one size, with a fringe of hairs under the head that looks
like a beard. Nests only in sandy soil, in a cleared circle of bare ground with
chaff around the entrance.

Why we wrote this page at all A pest control company that works one wet county in the far northwest corner of
Washington has no commercial reason to publish a page about an ant its customers
will almost never encounter.

title: Hobo Spider: What the Evidence Actually Says
sections:
Start with the correction The hobo spider is the most misrepresented animal in this county, and the
misrepresentation runs in the direction that sells treatments. So the correction
goes at the top rather than buried under a description.
How the reputation was built The claim has a specific origin, and knowing it helps explain why it stuck.
What the follow-up found Three separate lines of work went after the claim, and none of them supported it.
Why the correction has not reached most people Because retractions do not travel the way alarms do.
What the animal actually is Now the biology, which is genuinely interesting once the alarm is off the table.
How common it actually is here Less common than the name recognition suggests, and this matters.

Why you cannot identify one, and neither can we We get asked to confirm hobo spiders constantly, usually from a photograph, and
the honest answer is almost always that it cannot be done.
What a bite is and is not Nobody has much data, because verified bites are rare.

Where they turn up in this county's housing If you want to know whether funnel weavers are living around your building, the
places to look are consistent and none of them are in a bedroom.

When you actually see them The seasonal pattern here is the same one that drives every spider call in this
county, and it is worth being precise about what it is.

Why we say this warrants no treatment The verdict at the top of this page is that treating for hobo spiders is rarely
warranted, and it follows from everything above.

If you want one identified anyway Catch it under a glass with a piece of card slid beneath, and put it into a small
jar of rubbing alcohol if you want it kept. Alcohol preserves the structures that
matter; a spider flattened on a tissue usually cannot be worked on at all.

What you will not hear from us We will not tell you that the spider in your window well is a medical threat,
because the state health department says it is not.

title: Honey Bees: Why We Do Not Treat Them
sections:
The short version, first We do not treat honey bees. Not in a tree, not in a swarm on a fence post, and
not in a wall.

The question that decides everything: swarm or colony There are exactly two situations, they look superficially similar to somebody who
has not seen both, and they call for completely different responses.

Swarms: the situation that needs nobody A swarm is how a honey bee colony reproduces. When a hive outgrows its cavity,
the existing queen leaves with a large share of the workers, and the colony left
behind raises a new queen. The departing group flies a short distance — often
only a hundred yards or two — settles on the first convenient object, and forms a
cluster while scout bees go out looking

Established colonies in a structure This is the situation this page exists for, and it is a building problem wearing
an insect costume.

Why killing a wall colony is the wrong answer This is the part worth reading even if you are inclined to skip to the end,
because it is the decision people most often get wrong and the one that costs
the most.

What a proper removal actually involves The correct resolution for an established colony is a cut-out, and it is honest
to say up front that it is a real piece of work.

The chimney case, which is its own problem Flues deserve a paragraph of their own because they are the single most common
structural colony site on older housing here and the least forgiving one.

What people try first, and why it backfires Almost every difficult honey bee job we hear about got harder because of
something done in the first week.

Who to call Start with the WSU Honey Bees and Pollinators Program, which maintains a
county-by-county list of swarm removal contacts for Washington — beekeeping
associations with swarm teams, and individual collectors. The beekeepers
association covering Whatcom County is the other route to the same people, and
for a swarm hanging in the open it is usually the only call you need to make.

Honey bee or bumble bee The two get confused in both directions, and the practical consequence is small
because the answer is the same either way — but the reasoning differs.

A little biology, because it explains the behavior A honey bee worker has a barbed sting that tears free along with the venom sac
when it is used, and the bee dies. That is the reason a foraging honey bee is
reluctant to sting anything that is not directly threatening the colony — it is a
one-time act with a fatal cost, and the insect behaves accordingly. A yellowjacket
has no such constraint, whi

Keeping a colony from moving in Scouts are looking for a dry enclosed cavity of the right volume with a small,
defensible entrance. Buildings offer plenty, and the ones that get colonies tend
to get them more than once.

What we will actually do **Identify it, at no charge.** A photograph usually settles it in under a minute,
and a large share of these calls end right there with advice and no service.
If somebody in the household is allergic This changes the urgency without changing the recommendation.

Related work Most calls that begin as bees end at
[wasp and hornet control](/services/wasp-control/), and the ground-nesting
species behind that is the [western
yellowjacket](/pest-library/western-yellowjacket/). Our position on bees
generally, including bumble bees, mason bees and mining bees, is set out on
[bee removal](/services/bee-removal/). Round clean holes in fascia or deck rails
are a dif

title: House Mouse (Mus musculus) in Whatcom County
sections:
What a house mouse is *Mus musculus* is small, gray-brown above and only slightly paler beneath, with
small eyes, a pointed muzzle and a tail about as long as its head and body
together that is nearly hairless and the same color all the way round. An adult
weighs less than an ounce. Cornell's rodent identification guidance gives the
body at roughly two and a half to just under four inches, with th

House mouse or deer mouse This is the one identification on the page that changes the health advice, so it
goes near the top.
A quarter of an inch, and a coin that is not The single number worth carrying around is a quarter of an inch.

Thirty feet, and why it changes the whole job UC IPM records that house mice seldom venture more than thirty feet from their
nest site and food supply. That one behavioral fact explains most of what is
peculiar about mouse work.

The arithmetic nobody expects Two sets of figures explain why "there was only one" is not the reassurance it
sounds like.

Where they nest here Mice nest in something soft, dark and within a few steps of food. In Whatcom
County housing that is a short and predictable list.

Signs, in the order they usually appear Mice are quiet, small and mostly nocturnal, so the evidence generally arrives
before the animal does.

Shared buildings, where one unit is never the whole story Mice are the dominant rodent in apartments, duplexes and the student rental belt
around campus, and shared construction changes what a solution has to cover.

What mice do to insulation Mouse damage in an attic or a crawlspace looks different from rat damage and is
frequently underestimated because of it.

What house mice carry, and what they do not **They do not carry the hantavirus Washington reports.** This is the correction
worth making loudly, because the internet is careless about it. The Washington
State Department of Health states that hantavirus-infected deer mice excrete the
virus in urine, saliva and droppings, that infected deer mice live throughout the
state, that people are at risk any

Trapping, and where it goes wrong Mice are, helpfully, the opposite of rats on the one behavior that matters most.
Rats avoid new objects for days. Mice investigate them, sometimes within hours of
placement. So a mouse trap line that is set correctly usually produces results the
first night, and a line that produces nothing for a week is telling you something
about the setting rather than about th

Bait, and the two reasons for caution Rodenticide has a legitimate role in exterior and commercial pressure management.
Inside a house with mice it is usually the wrong tool, for two separate reasons
worth stating rather than implying.

The season, and the honest verdict Mouse pressure in this county climbs from late September, runs hard through
October and November and stays elevated all winter. What changes is not the number
of mice outdoors but the relative appeal of a heated building once cover has died
back and outdoor food has declined. A house that was untroubled all summer and
has mice in the second week of October did no

When it is not a house mouse If the animal has a white belly with a hard edge to it and a two-tone furry tail,
it is a deer mouse, and the cleanup guidance above matters more rather than less.

Where to start Tell us what you have found and where, leave a representative patch of droppings
undisturbed if you reasonably can, and get dry goods into rigid sealed containers
in the meantime. Somebody will look at the building rather than the room — the
connected voids, the crawlspace with a light, the exterior at ground level — and
give you a plain account of the entry points, the trap plan, a

title: Indianmeal Moth (Plodia interpunctella) — Pantry Moth
sections:
This is one package, not a house An Indianmeal moth infestation is a container of food. It is almost never a
building problem, it is almost never a hygiene problem, and it is almost never
worth treating a room over.
The moth itself Small, and unmistakable once you have looked at one properly.
Webbing is the evidence The insects are hard to see inside food. What they leave is not.

The wandering, and why people search the wrong place This is the behavior that sends households in the wrong direction, and it is
worth understanding because it saves an enormous amount of pointless searching.

Where the source actually hides Kitchens get emptied first and the source is frequently not in the kitchen. In
rough order of how often it turns out to be the answer:

It was probably in the package before you bought it This is worth saying because people are embarrassed about these calls and they
should not be.

The season here Development runs on temperature, and a heated Whatcom County kitchen is warm
year-round, so this species never really stops.
Around the county Where the source turns out to be tracks the kind of property more than the town.
Not the clothes moth, and not a weevil Two separations worth making quickly.

Clearing it out The sequence matters, because doing it in the wrong order is how the "we threw
everything away and it came back" case happens.

Why nobody should spray your pantry UC IPM is unambiguous, and we agree with it entirely: insecticides are not
recommended for controlling pantry pests, and spraying pesticides on or near food
may cause greater harm to a household than the pantry pests would.

When we are actually worth calling The verdict on this page is *rarely-warranted*, and we mean it. Most households
solve this themselves once they know where to look, and the pages you are reading
exist partly so that they can.

Knowing when it is over Because adults keep appearing for a while after the source has gone, households
routinely conclude the clearance failed when it did not. A few markers help.
Where to start Before you call, do three things.

title: Millipedes Indoors in Whatcom County
sections:
This is a weather event, and it has already ended A millipede in your hallway is not living there. It cannot live there. It got in
during a wet week, it is losing water through its cuticle faster than it can
replace it, and there is nothing inside a heated house that it eats.

Two pairs of legs, and why that one detail matters Nearly every unnecessary call about this animal comes from confusing it with a
centipede, so this section is the practical core of the page.

Why this profile has no binomial Every other entry in this library names a species. This one names a group, and
that is deliberate rather than lazy.

What one actually looks like **Shape.** Long, segmented and round in cross-section — Penn State describes the
body as cylindrical and wire-like. Under a hard outer shell, which is what makes
the coiled ones feel like small springs when you sweep them.
The autumn migration The pattern here is seasonal, dramatic and entirely normal.
So: get a broom Written as its own section because it is the recommendation, not a throwaway.

What actually changes next autumn The work that reduces next year's event is outdoor, cheap and unglamorous. All
of it is about how much habitat sits against the building and how wet it stays.

Millipedes and pillbugs The two get mixed up constantly, they turn up under the same board, and the
answer for both is the same — but they are not remotely the same animal.

Which properties get hit hardest Three property types account for most of the heavy events we hear about, and the
common factor is depth of organic material rather than anything about the house.

Things that do not work **Interior baseboard sprays.** The animals are transient and dying. There is
nothing behind the wall to reach.

The wider group this belongs to Millipedes sit in a small set of animals that share one requirement and one
message. Silverfish, sowbugs, pillbugs, springtails and the moisture-following
ants all need sustained damp, none of them can hold a population in a dry space,
and none of them causes structural harm on its own.
When it is genuinely worth treating Having spent the page recommending a broom, here is the honest other side.

What the migration tells you about the building The insect itself is telling you almost nothing — millipedes coming to a
foundation after heavy rain is what happens on healthy ground with a healthy
litter layer, and a garden that produces them is a garden that is decomposing
properly.

What we will not sell you **A treatment for insects that are already dying.** Everything indoors during a
migration is on a two-day clock.

What to tell us if you call anyway **Which animal.** Slow and coiling, or fast with long legs. That single detail
sends the conversation in two completely different directions.

title: Moisture Ants (Lasius) in Whatcom County
sections:
An insect that functions as a measuring instrument Most species in this library are here because of what they do to a building.
This one earns its place because of what it tells you about one.

What they look like Small, and that is the first thing. WSU gives pest species of this group as
three to five millimeters — roughly an eighth to a fifth of an inch, which is a
fraction of a carpenter ant. Workers are monomorphic, so unlike carpenter ants
every individual in the column is the same size as every other.
The carton nest The second identification is the material, and it is genuinely distinctive.

The swarm is usually the first anyone knows Almost nobody discovers this species by finding a worker. What happens instead is
that a room suddenly fills with small winged ants.

What the presence of the colony actually proves This is where the species pays for itself, so it is worth being precise about the
chain of events rather than waving at "damp".

Where the water is, in this county The locations repeat, and the reason is climatic rather than anything to do with
how a house is kept. Around thirty-five inches of rain spread across a long mild
season means timber that gets wet here has no hot dry stretch in which to give the
water back. A wall assembly that would recover in a fortnight in a continental
climate can stay above the decay threshol

Why the treatment verdict on this page is "depends" WSU's position is that chemical control is rarely advised for this group, and the
verdict on this page could reasonably have read that way. It does not, and the
reasoning is worth setting out because the deciding factor is not what the label
suggests.
What they live on, and the lawn ants you can ignore A point that surprises people: this group is not feeding on the wood either.

Reading the wood yourself Most of what a technician does with a suspect member can be done by a homeowner
with a flashlight and a screwdriver, and doing it before anyone visits shortens
the conversation considerably.

What we will not sell you **A treatment instead of a repair.** It does not hold, and it quiets the one
signal that was pointing at the decay.

What else lives with them A cavity wet enough for this species supports a whole community, and recognizing
the company is part of reading the finding.

Telling them apart from carpenter ants The two get confused in both directions and the distinction changes the entire
response, so it is worth having straight.

The one prevention measure that matters Everything on the usual list — sealing entry points, moving woodpiles, trimming
vegetation — is secondary here to a single item, and it is not a pest control
measure.

title: Mud Daubers: The Mud Tubes Under Your Eaves
sections:
What you are looking at A hard tube of dried mud, roughly the length and thickness of a finger, stuck
to a wall in a place that stays dry. Sometimes one. Sometimes a dozen laid side
by side and plastered over into a lump the size of a fist.

The three kinds, and the two you will actually meet **The black-and-yellow mud dauber**, *Sceliphron caementarium*, is the one most
people find. Long thread waist, black with yellow markings and yellow legs. She
builds cells one at a time out of mud, sets them side by side, and then plasters
the whole group over so the finished nest is a rounded lump rather than a set of
visible tubes.

Where she builds The requirement is a vertical or overhead surface that stays dry and sheltered,
and that narrows it down to a predictable set of places on any property.
Spiders, which is the interesting part Every cell is a larder, and what is in the larder is spiders.

Why we usually tell you to leave it alone Because there is nothing to treat, and the extension guidance says so about as
plainly as extension guidance ever says anything.
How to take them off Wet the nest first if you want less dust, then scrape.
Preventing them, honestly There is not much, and we would rather say so than sell a plan.

What the old nests attract afterwards This is the one part of the story that occasionally does matter, and it is why
clearing nests off an outbuilding is not purely cosmetic.

Telling a mud dauber apart from what actually matters The whole practical value of this page is helping somebody sort a harmless
solitary wasp from the two or three that are not, and the material each builds
with does most of the work.

Around this county Mud daubers are ordinary here without being the thing anybody calls first. We
see them most in the places the rest of this page predicts: carports and open
garages, barns and equipment sheds on rural property, the underside of decks,
and pump houses.
What this tells you about the building Very little, and that is unusual for this site.

What we will not sell you We will not treat mud dauber nests. If we are on your property for something
else and there are nests on the carport ceiling, we will knock them down for you
and not put it on the invoice.

The one place a mud dauber nest is genuinely a hazard Everything above says this insect is harmless, and it is. The nest is a
different question in exactly one situation, and it is worth its own heading
because almost nobody knows about it.

The year, and when the nests appear She is active through the warm months, building and provisioning from roughly
early summer to the end of August in this county.
Finding one indoors It happens, and it is not a sign that anything is nesting in the house.

Clearing an outbuilding, practically Where nests have built up over several seasons in a barn, a carport or a shop,
the job is worth doing properly once rather than picking at it.

A last word on the nests you cannot reach Some mud dauber nests are simply out of reach — high in a barn, on a rafter over
stored equipment, on the underside of a bridge deck or a dock structure. If they
are not blocking anything and nobody has to walk under them, the honest answer is
to leave them there rather than hire access equipment to remove something
harmless. We would rather say that than

title: Asian Lady Beetle — The One That Bites and Stains
sections:
The ladybug that is not a ladybug Every October the same call comes in from all over this county. Hundreds — sometimes
thousands — of orange beetles covering a wall that gets the afternoon sun, working
their way into the gaps around trim and vents, and then turning up indoors on the
warm days of late winter.

Recognizing one Do not look at the spots. The name is literal: this beetle ranges from pale
yellow-orange through to deep red, and carries anywhere from no spots at all to
eighteen. Two individuals from the same wall can look like different species.

Why they are on the south wall The behavior is specific enough to predict, and understanding it is what makes
the timing of any treatment work.
What actually happens indoors Nothing, is the honest answer, until it warms up.

The bite Native lady beetles are, for practical purposes, incapable of bothering anyone.
This one is different, and the extension literature is consistent about it.

The stain, and why not to squash them When disturbed, the beetle releases a yellow fluid from its leg joints. The term
for it is reflex bleeding, and it is the insect's defense.

Allergies, and the part nobody mentions Continued exposure to these beetles inside a building can produce genuine
allergic responses in some people. Penn State lists rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma
and facial angioedema. Minnesota notes that exposure to dead beetles in a
building can cause allergic reactions.

Pets Penn State records that animals which consume these beetles may sustain
chemical burns inside the mouth.

Why we will not spray your wall voids This is the most important practical point on the page and it is the one that
costs us work.
What does work, and when Two things, and both of them happen before the beetles arrive.

So why is our answer "depends" Because the honest recommendation varies with the building, and this site
labels every species with what it actually warrants rather than with what we
would like to sell.

Around this county This is one of the two insects the owner of this company names when asked what
autumn looks like here, the other being the brown marmorated stink bug, and the
two arrive on the same walls within days of each other.

What it is doing the rest of the year Worth saying, because it changes how people feel about the insect and because
it is true: for eight months of the year this beetle is doing something useful.

The short version It is not the ladybug you remember; it is an introduced relative that
overwinters in buildings. It gathers on sun-facing walls in early October and
gets in through ordinary gaps. It does not breed indoors, eat anything, or
damage the structure.

One more note on timing The window for exterior work is genuinely narrow and it moves with the weather
rather than the date, so it is worth booking on a forecast rather than on a
calendar. The trigger is the first run of cold nights followed by a warm, still
afternoon, which is when the beetles gather on sunlit walls in numbers. Treat
before that and the residual has weathered; treat after it and

title: Norway Rat (Rattus norvegicus) in Whatcom County
sections:
The rat that is actually here Washington has exactly two established rat species, and both arrived on ships.
WSU Extension puts it plainly: the Norway rat and the black rat, neither of them
native, both of them here long enough that nobody thinks of them as introduced
any more. Of the two, the Norway rat is what turns up in most Whatcom County
buildings.

Norway rat or roof rat The two get written about as though they were interchangeable, and they are not.
Sending somebody into an attic to look for a Norway rat wastes an afternoon;
sending them into a crawlspace to look for a [roof
rat](/pest-library/roof-rat/) wastes the same afternoon in the other direction.

Where it lives on a Whatcom County property Start outside and low. Blackberry is the single best rat habitat this county
produces, and there is a great deal of it — thickets along creek corridors, the
back of a greenbelt, the fence line nobody has cut for six years. Woodpiles
stacked on soil. Sheds set on skids. The dead space beneath a deck. Compost that
is a heap rather than a bin. Stacked palle

Reading a burrow Burrows are the best evidence a property gives you and almost nobody looks for
them, because they sit at ankle height against a foundation and under vegetation.

The year, which runs on rain first and then cold Two mechanisms, in that order, and most accounts of autumn rats only carry the
second one.
Half an inch, a quarter inch, and the dime that is wrong Numbers matter here more than adjectives, so here are the ones that hold up.

What the damage actually is **Wiring.** Cable sheathing is a chewable material sitting in exactly the spaces
this animal occupies. It is the damage with the worst tail risk and the one
nobody can see from inside the house.

Insulation, and the honest version of that conversation Fiberglass under a floor is the best nesting material most buildings contain, and
an established crawlspace population does three things to it. It pulls batts down
out of the joist bays to build with. It compresses what remains into flattened
runs. And it saturates the material with urine, after which the fibers settle and
stay settled.

What a Norway rat carries, and what it does not This is worth getting exactly right, because the risk that gets attached to rats
in popular writing is frequently the wrong one.

Trapping, including where it fails Trapping is how anything inside a building envelope gets removed, and it is a
skill rather than a purchase. It also fails in specific, repeatable ways, which
are worth naming.

Rodenticide, stated with the risk attached Bait has a place on the exterior of a property under real pressure, and the
reason to discuss it openly is that the risk it carries is not to the rat.

Exclusion is the half that lasts The verdict at the top of this page says we treat this, and that is true. It
would be dishonest to leave it there.
When it is not a Norway rat at all Two corrections worth making before anyone treats.

What the work looks like Someone goes the length of the crawlspace with a light rather than reporting from
the hatch, walks the exterior at ground level, and reads the burrows, runs and
droppings for size, age and direction. That produces a mapped list of openings
and a realistic account of how long this has been running.

title: Odorous House Ants — Tapinoma sessile
sections:
The smell test There is no other insect in this library that identifies itself by odor, and
this one does it so reliably that it is worth leading with.

What it is native, and what that changes This is a North American native, not an import, and the distinction has practical
weight. Utah State records natural colonies containing something like fifteen to
thirty workers — a genuinely small woodland ant living under bark and stones,
tending aphids and getting on with a modest life.

Why a spray makes it worse This is the single most consequential thing on the page, and it is the reason so
many households arrive at a professional with more ants than they started with.

Where the nests actually are The species nests opportunistically, in existing spaces rather than excavated
ones, which is why the list is so long and why a single visit does not always find
every one of them.

Why they came in The trigger is almost always weather rather than housekeeping, and it helps to
know which pattern you are in.

What they cost you, honestly Nothing structural. WSU is explicit that this species causes no structural damage,
and it is worth saying so plainly on a pest control company's website, because
this ant is routinely sold against as though it were a threat to the building.
Why the verdict here is "depends", and on what Two situations, and the difference between them is easy to establish.

What correct treatment involves **Identify before choosing anything.** The smell test plus the hidden node takes
under a minute and it determines the entire approach, since the response for this
species is close to the opposite of the response for a carpenter ant.

How fast the population rebuilds Part of why this species outlasts casual efforts is arithmetic, and the numbers
are worth having.

The six things people have already tried Almost everyone has done something before calling, and it helps to know what each
of them actually accomplished.

The year, as this species runs it here **February and March.** Overwintering nests break up as temperatures rise and
subcolonies redistribute. The first indoor sightings of the year are usually a
few scouts rather than a column.

How to tell whether it actually worked Worth stating, because the failure mode with this species is a household
concluding too early that a treatment did not take.

Telling them apart **Carpenter ants.** Not a close call once you look. Carpenter ant workers run from
a quarter inch to a half inch and vary in size within the same nest; these are
uniform and around three millimeters. Carpenter ants are black with reddish legs
and produce fibrous frass below slit-shaped openings in timber. Crushed carpenter
ants do not smell of coconut. And the implication is ent

The short version Small, uniformly sized, brown-black, one hidden waist node, and unmistakable when
crushed. It will not damage your house. It will not respond well to anything you
spray at it, and spraying is the one intervention with a documented mechanism for
making the situation worse. Bait it, feed it nothing else, close the route once it
has gone quiet, and deal with the aphids on the shrubs

title: Pacific Dampwood Termite in Whatcom County
sections:
The termite that actually lives here Type a question about termites into a search engine and almost everything that
comes back describes an insect that does not live in northwest Washington. The
material is about aggressive soil-nesting species in the South and Southeast:
shelter tubes climbing a foundation, chemical soil barriers, perimeter bait
stations, tented houses. That content dominates bec
What it looks like Most people meet this insect in one form and never see the other two.

Telling them from winged carpenter ants This is the identification that goes wrong most often in Whatcom County, and it
goes wrong in both directions. Carpenter ant swarmers are also large, also
winged, also alarming, and also turn up around a building. Three field marks
separate them and none needs magnification.

When you will see them, and why it is autumn The flight season here runs late. WSU Extension describes swarming flights on
warm evenings in late summer or fall, especially after rains, and that matches
what we get called about — a mild September or early October evening, a day or
two after a wet spell, with alates coming to a porch light, a lit window, or a
security lamp over a garage door.
What the finding actually means Here is the part that separates this species from everything you have read.

Where they turn up in Whatcom County buildings The locations are predictable because they follow water, and in this county
water follows the same short list of building defects.

When they are in a stump rather than the house A fair share of dampwood findings in this county are not in a building at all,
and the right answer for those is different.
Reading the damage Opened timber tells you which insect you have even when nothing is moving.

What treatment involves The shape of the work is set by the biology, and it is unlike the soil-barrier
approach that dominates termite marketing.

What you get in writing, and what you do not Worth being exact about, because this is where pest control companies are
routinely vague.

What we will not sell you **A soil barrier for a dampwood colony.** No soil dependency, no colony in the
ground, no mechanism. Treating the perimeter of a house for an insect in a wet
header is money aimed at the wrong place.

Keeping them out, which is really water management Every preventive measure for this species is a building maintenance task. That
is the honest summary of the whole page.
How urgent this is, honestly Somewhere between the two extremes people arrive with.

Related work The insect biology and the county-wide picture sit on our
[termite and wood-destroying pest page](/services/termite-control/). Where the
finding is in a crawl area, [dampwood termites in a
crawlspace](/services/termite-control/dampwood-termites-in-a-crawlspace/) goes
through what the space itself is telling you. Where it is at a window,
[soft wood around a window
sill](/services/termi

title: Pavement Ant (Tetramorium immigrans) in Whatcom County
sections:
The craters give it away before the ant does Most species in this library are identified from the insect. This one is usually
identified from the dirt.

What it looks like under a lens Get one onto white paper and the ant itself is unremarkable at arm's length —
small, dark, and easy to file mentally under "the little black ants."

The sidewalk wars This is the behavior people actually ask us about, and it is worth the space
because the answer is reassuring and almost nobody gives it.

Where the nest actually is Hard surfaces are the point. A slab holds heat into the evening, keeps rain off
the soil beneath it, gives a stable roof over a gallery system, and provides a
clean edge to travel along. From the ant's side of it, a residential driveway is
close to ideal habitat.

Why it is always the ground floor The way this species enters a building follows directly from where it lives, and
it produces a pattern that is worth recognizing because it narrows the search
enormously.

One queen, and what that changes There is a structural fact about this species that decides most of the practical
advice, and it is the opposite of the situation with the odorous house ant.

What they actually cost you Very little, and it is worth being plain about that on a pest control company's
website.

Why this page says "depends", and on what The verdict above is genuinely split, and the line between the two sides is easy
to draw.

What competent work looks like **Identify first.** The two waist nodes and the grooved head take under a minute
and they determine everything after. Getting this wrong in the other direction —
treating a pavement ant as though it were an odorous house ant, or the reverse —
is the most common reason an ant job needs doing twice.

The things people have already tried **A retail aerosol along the trail.** Kills what it touches and erases the
pheromone route that would have led to the nest. Less damaging with this species
than with a multi-queen one, but it removes the best evidence in the room and
buys about a day.

The year, as this species runs it here **February and March.** Colonies come out of winter slowly. The first indoor
sightings are usually a handful of scouts along a baseboard on a mild day, and
they mean very little on their own.

Pavement ant or odorous house ant These two account for most of the small dark ants in Whatcom County kitchens,
and the difference decides how patient you have to be.

The short version Small, uniformly sized, dark, two waist nodes, a grooved head, a pair of spines,
and a heap of fine soil at a crack in your concrete. It will not hurt your
building. The spring battles on the sidewalk are normal and self-resolving.
Outdoors it is part of the landscape and worth leaving alone.

title: Pharaoh Ants: The One Spraying Makes Worse
sections:
The one where the obvious response backfires Most ant problems tolerate a bit of improvisation. Somebody sprays the trail, it
helps or it does not, and the situation is no worse for the attempt.
Recognizing them Small, yellow, and all one size.

Budding, and why it changes everything Nearly every ant most people meet reproduces the same way: winged reproductives
leave on a mating flight, mated queens land, shed their wings, and try to found
a colony alone. Most fail. That is why ordinary ant colonies are separate,
territorial, and beatable one at a time.
What actually works Bait, patiently, with nothing repellent used anywhere near it.

What they eat, and why that matters The extension list is worth quoting because its range is the point: bread,
cookies, cakes, sugar, syrup, liver, bacon and dead insects.

Where they turn up around here Pharaoh ants are an indoor species at this latitude — heated, occupied buildings
with year-round warmth. They do not overwinter outdoors in Whatcom County.

The multi-unit problem If pharaoh ants are in an attached building, unit-level treatment is close to
pointless and it is worth being blunt about that before anybody spends money.
Telling them from the others Four small ants get reported the same way and the differences matter.

Why we would rather see a sample The characters that separate these species are structural and small: antennal
segment counts, the shape and length of the antennal club, the number of nodes
in the waist, whether the surface is sculptured.

What a job looks like from your side **A first visit that mostly involves looking.** Trails traced, nest locations
inferred from where the trails go, food sources noted, and the building's
construction taken into account — especially in attached housing.

What we will not sell you We will not spray a building for pharaoh ants. If somebody quotes you a
perimeter treatment or a knockdown application for this species, they have
either misidentified it or they are about to make it worse, and either way that
is worth knowing before they arrive.

Why hospitals care about this ant specifically Pharaoh ants have a place in the medical and institutional pest literature that
almost no other ant has, and the reasons are worth setting out because they also
explain why the species is taken seriously in ordinary buildings.

The apartment problem, in detail Attached housing is where this ant does its worst work in an ordinary community,
and the mechanics are worth understanding by anybody in a building with shared
walls.
What to do before we arrive Small things, and they genuinely shorten the work.

Around this county We do not see pharaoh ants often here, and that is worth saying plainly rather
than implying a threat that is not there. The common indoor ant in Whatcom
County is the odorous house ant by a wide margin.
The one thing to take away If you remember nothing else from this page, remember the sequence.

A note on what "gone" means Because this species declines rather than stops, it is worth agreeing in advance
what the end of the job looks like.

title: Pillbugs: A Crustacean With a Breathing Problem
sections: The one fact that explains everything A pillbug is not an insect.
What one looks like Small, oval, armored, and instantly recognizable once you have the shape.

Pillbug or sowbug These two live under the same board, arrive at the same threshold, and get the
same answer, but they are different animals and the separation takes a second.
Pillbug or millipede The other regular confusion, and this one is not close once you look properly.

Where they actually live Outside, in the layer of decomposing material against damp ground, and the list
of preferred addresses is short and consistent.

The life cycle, briefly, because it is strange Worth two paragraphs because it is unlike anything else in this library and it
explains why the population is so persistent.
Why they come inside, and why they leave feet first Two triggers, both about water.

So: get a broom Written as its own heading because it is the recommendation rather than an
aside.

What actually changes next year The durable work is all outdoors, all cheap, and all about how much wet organic
material sits against the building.
What the pillbugs are telling you about the building Here is the part worth reading even if the animal itself does not interest you.

Where this happens around the county The property types that produce the heaviest arrivals have one thing in common,
and it is not the age or quality of the house. It is how much wet organic
material is banked against it.

The year, as it runs here **October into December.** The main event. Heavy rain onto ground that is
already loaded pushes them out of the litter layer, and the arrivals at
thresholds follow within a day or two of the weather. This is when the calls
come.

Things that do not work **Interior perimeter sprays.** Transient, dying animals with no reservoir behind
the wall.
When it is genuinely worth treating Having spent the page recommending a dustpan, the other side.

What we will not sell you **A treatment for animals that cannot breathe in your house.** Everything
indoors is on a few days' clock.

Related work The other slow armored animal at the same threshold is the
[millipede](/pest-library/millipede/), and the fast one with long legs is
covered on
[centipede and millipede control](/services/centipede-control/). If the
population is under the floor rather than in the yard, that is
[crawlspace cleanout and restoration](/services/crawlspace-restoration/). The
sealing is [exclusion and repa

title: Ponerine Ants: The Sting With No Ant In Sight
sections:
The ant you get stung by without seeing Most ant problems announce themselves. There is a trail, or a mound, or a
scattering of soil on a patio, and the insect responsible is available for
inspection.

What is actually happening The colony is underground, outside the living space, very often beneath a
concrete slab — a basement floor, a garage, a patio, a path, the pad under an
addition.
Recognizing them Small and unremarkable, which is part of the difficulty.
Why the sting is the whole story An ant sting at this size ought to be nothing, and this one is not.

The slab problem Here is the honest difficulty, and it is the reason this species has a
reputation among people who do this work.

Why potted plants get a mention The extension guidance includes a specific and slightly unexpected piece of
advice: inspect potted plants for the possible introduction of these ants into a
residential area.
Telling them apart from the small ants that matter more Four small indoor ants get reported similarly and the responses differ.

Around this county The species is established in urban areas across the Pacific Northwest, which
includes ours, and the circumstances that produce a call are specific.

What we would actually do **Establish what stung you**, which usually means the circumstances rather than a
specimen, because the insect is rarely retained. Where there is a specimen, it
settles it quickly.

What we will not sell you We will not promise to eliminate a colony under a concrete slab. It may be
possible where there is access; where there is not, saying so is the only
honest position, and a recurring treatment sold against an unreachable nest is a
subscription rather than a solution.

Why this species is hard to name for a customer There is an awkwardness in explaining this ant to somebody who has just been
stung, and it is worth acknowledging.

What makes them different from every other ant here Two things, and both run against the pattern the rest of this library
establishes.
What to do in the moment If winged insects are emerging into a room:

Slab-on-grade, and why this is a construction question The reason this species has a page rather than a paragraph is that the buildings
it exploits are a recognizable category, and knowing that lets somebody predict
the problem rather than react to it.

What the emergence season looks like The pattern people report is a cluster rather than a season, and it is worth
setting expectations about it.

What a visit costs and what it should produce We would rather set the expectation for this one in advance, because it is a
species where a customer can easily pay for a result nobody can deliver.

The short version Tiny winged insects indoors, at a window or a light, in a room over a slab. A
sting that hurts far more than the size of the thing suggests. No trail, no
foraging, nothing found when anybody goes looking.

title: Rodent Mites — Bites After the Rodents Are Gone
sections:
The call this page exists for Somebody starts getting itchy marks overnight. It is one room, usually a
bedroom, often upstairs. Nothing has changed — no travel, no secondhand
furniture, no guest. The bed has been stripped and searched more than once and
there is nothing on it. A bed bug treatment has sometimes already happened and
made no difference at all.

Bites do not identify anything, here or anywhere Before any of the rest of it, the same principle that governs our
[bed bug](/pest-library/bed-bug/) page governs this one, and it cuts both ways.

What a rodent mite actually is A mite is not an insect. It is an arachnid — Minnesota Extension gives the adult
form as two main body parts and eight legs — and the practical consequence is
that it does not look or move like anything you have a mental picture of.

Why they leave the nest A mite on a living rodent has no reason to go anywhere. The host is warm, it
returns to the nest, and the whole life cycle runs inside a space the size of a
grapefruit.

The timeline is the strongest evidence you have Almost nobody arrives at this diagnosis from the insect. They arrive at it from
the sequence, and it is worth writing yours down before anybody visits.

Describing the skin symptoms, not diagnosing them We are not medically qualified and this section is written accordingly. What
follows is what the extension and public health sources describe, and it stops
there.

Why bed bug treatment does nothing here This is the practical center of the page and it is worth being explicit about
the mechanism, because "it will not work" is less convincing than why.

It is self-limiting, but only after the nest is gone There is genuinely good news in this and it deserves its own section, because
people arrive at this page frightened that they have acquired something
permanent.

Confirming it, which is worth doing properly **Collect something.** Clear tape pressed onto a pale surface where you have
felt something, or onto skin, or run along a windowsill or a headboard. Texas
A&M notes these mites can be picked up with wet fingers or sticky tape. A
specimen settles in a minute what a description circles around for half an hour.

Where the nest actually is The search follows the rodent rather than the mite, and in Whatcom County
housing the shortlist is familiar.

What the work involves **A structural search rather than a bedroom one.** The attic, the soffits, the
roofline, the wall voids and the crawlspace, looking for current or recent
occupation. This is a different job from a bed bug search and it goes to
different parts of the building.

The disease question, kept in proportion There is a real association here and it is worth stating accurately rather than
either omitting it or leaning on it.
When the nest is a bird's This is the boundary worth being clear about before anybody books anything.

What else produces the same complaint **Bed bugs**, obviously, and the search that rules them in or out is a real
piece of work with definite evidence attached — spotting, shed skins, eggs.
That is the [bed bug](/pest-library/bed-bug/) page.

What we will not do **Treat a bedroom on suspicion.** Applying product around where somebody sleeps
without an established cause is not a neutral act, and if the cause is not an
arthropod it changes nothing except the bill.

Where to start Tell us the sequence — when the biting started, which room, who is affected, and
what was happening in the building in the month before. The rodent history is
the part people leave out because they think it was resolved, and it is
frequently the most important sentence in the conversation.

title: Roof Rat (Rattus rattus) in Whatcom County
sections:
The other rat Most rat content treats the animal as a single species with a single set of
habits, and in a county with both of ours that assumption sends people to the
wrong half of the building.

Telling the two apart in thirty seconds The differences are not subtle once you know what to compare, and UC IPM sets
them out in exactly the terms that are usable in the field.

Where they turn up in this county WDFW gives the distribution note that matters locally: roof rats prefer
saltwater-influenced warmer climates and are often seen in port cities and
coastal towns. That is a description of the western edge of this county.

Fruit, nuts and what feeds a climber UC IPM records that roof rats travel up to three hundred feet or more for food,
and this species has an old and well-earned reputation for fruit.

Signs, read from below Very few people find this by going into the attic. It announces itself in other
ways.

The attic insulation problem An attic is a hostile place to live. It is hot in July, cold in January, and a
long way from anything to eat. What makes it worth the climb is the insulation,
which from the animal's point of view is a warehouse of soft, dry, warm, endlessly
available building material.

What the damage adds up to The nuisance case for dealing with this is the noise. The actual case is what
gets chewed while nobody can see it.

The timing of it here The seasonal curve is the same one that governs everything else in this county,
and it is driven by water and cover rather than by temperature. Pressure builds
from late September, peaks through October and November, and stays elevated
through a winter that never resets anything.

False ceilings, shared roofs and commercial buildings The roof rat's preference for horizontal voids off the ground makes it
disproportionately a commercial and multifamily problem, and those buildings fail
in ways a single-family house does not.

The numbers, and one comparison to retire Roof rats are smaller than Norway rats and the exclusion threshold does not
change for it.

Trapping a climber Everything about trapping this species is a variation on one point: the animal is
not on the floor.

What a roof rat carries WDFW lists bubonic plague, salmonella, leptospirosis and tularemia among the
diseases spread from Old World rats to people. That is the accurate general
statement and it is worth reading with proportion: the everyday mechanism in a
Whatcom County house is contamination of food and surfaces, not anything dramatic.

Exclusion at height Closing a roofline is the same discipline as closing a foundation performed
somewhere less convenient, and the difference in convenience is most of why it
gets skipped.

When it is not a roof rat Daytime noise overhead, heavier than a rat, is usually something else. Squirrels
are the common mistake and they are not rodent work as we scope it; bats and
birds sit further outside it again, with legal timing attached. We will tell you
what your description sounds like and point you toward somebody equipped for it,
and it costs nothing to ask.

Getting it looked at The useful visit walks the roofline from outside, gets into the roof space where
it is safe to do so, checks the tree and utility contact, and then checks the
crawlspace anyway — because a meaningful share of attic activity arrives from
below through a wall rather than over the roof.

title: Sawtoothed Grain Beetle (Oryzaephilus surinamensis)
sections:
The whole problem is one container A sawtoothed grain beetle infestation is a package of food that has been in the
house too long, or arrived already carrying the insect. It is not a structural
problem, it is not a hygiene problem, and it is very seldom a treatment problem.

What it looks like Small, flat and slender, which is a different silhouette from most beetles people
meet indoors.

Flat is not a detail, it is the mechanism The most common question about this insect is how it got into a bag that had
never been opened, and the answer is that it did not need to open one.
What it eats, and a genuine disagreement between sources The food list is broad and skewed toward processed material.

How fast it moves, and how long it lasts The numbers explain both why an infestation escalates and why it takes patience
to be sure of a clearance.

Where the source hides The kitchen shelf is the last place to look, not the first. In rough order of how
often each turns out to be the answer:

What it actually costs you, and what it does not Worth being precise here, because the internet is bad at this and the anxiety it
generates is disproportionate to the insect.

Beetle, weevil, or moth Three things turn up in the same cupboard and are cleared the same way, but
telling them apart tells you what to search for.

Carpet beetle or grain beetle This is the confusion this profile is cross-linked for, and two questions settle
it.

Clearing it Order matters, because doing it backward is how a household ends up doing it
twice.

Why nobody should spray your food storage UC IPM states that insecticides are not recommended for controlling pantry pests,
and that spraying pesticides on or near food may cause greater harm to a
household than the pantry pests themselves would. That is a land-grant program
saying the quiet part out loud and we will not soften it.
When calling us is the right move Most of these do not need us and this page is written so that they do not.

Knowing when it is finished Adults live long enough that stragglers mean less than people assume, so it helps
to know which signals carry weight.

What we will not do **Spray a pantry, fog a kitchen, or treat a shelf that food goes back onto.**
Food storage does not get product on it, and UC IPM's position on that is
unambiguous.

Where to start **Keep a specimen.** A beetle in a small sealed bag or a close photograph settles
in seconds what a description circles around for twenty minutes. The toothed
thorax is visible in a phone macro shot.

title: Silverfish (Lepisma) in Whatcom County
sections:
The insect is the gauge, not the fault There is a version of this page that would open by describing what silverfish
chew and how quickly they multiply. It would be accurate and it would send you
in the wrong direction.

What you have in front of you **Shape.** Flat, tapering from a broad head end to a narrow tail, which people
describe as teardrop or carrot-shaped. Wingless.

A note on the name The binomial has moved, and it is worth stating plainly because the two spellings
sit side by side in the reference literature and look like a mistake.
The humidity range, and what dropping it achieves This is the operative section.

Buy the hygrometer before anything else An inexpensive digital hygrometer costs less than a single service visit and it
settles arguments that otherwise run for years.

Where the water is coming from The sources of the humidity are boringly consistent across this county, and none
of them is exotic.
What they eat, and where the loss is real Not the house. Starch, and the things starch is in.
The bathtub is a bucket Worth its own note, because it produces a badly distorted impression of numbers.

Firebrats read the opposite way A firebrat is the same body plan pointed at the other end of the thermometer,
and the distinction changes where you look rather than what you do.

Why the verdict here is "depends" Two of the three species in this humidity group get a plainer verdict than this
one. This page does not, and the reasoning is worth setting out.

Storage, which does more than treatment for the things you care about If the loss is paper or fabric, this section is worth more to you than anything
else here.
What a silverfish finding says about the building This is the part that matters after the insects are gone.

The company they keep A space wet enough for silverfish supports a small community, and recognizing it
saves a second call.

When in the year to look The seasonal shape here is shallow, because the reservoir is indoors and largely
buffered from the weather. But there is one timing point that is genuinely
useful and almost nobody uses it.

What it is not A short list, because the wrong identification sends the whole job somewhere
else.

What we will not sell you **A treatment schedule instead of a dehumidifier.** If the honest answer to your
call is a machine and a working extractor fan, that is what you will be told, on
the phone, before anyone books anything.

Doing it yourself, in order **One: measure.** Hygrometer in the affected room and in the space below it.
Read it across a wet month.

title: Thatching Ants: The Mound Builders That Bite
sections:
What you are looking at A low dome in a sunny part of the yard, built out of dried grass, conifer
needles and small stems rather than soil, with large ants working over the
surface. The mound may be a foot across or it may be waist high. It is usually
in an open spot that gets sun, on a bank, at a woodland edge, along a fence
line, or in rough ground beside a driveway.

Recognizing them [PNW 624](https://pubs.extension.wsu.edu/product/identification-and-habits-of-key-ant-pests-in-the-pacific-northwest/), the WSU, OSU and University of Idaho extension key for this region,
gives the identification in a few lines and they are worth quoting closely
because the details are what separate this ant from the one people fear.

The mound, and what it is for The thatch is the defining behavior. The ants gather plant material — most often
grass, and needles where there are conifers — and pile it over a nest excavated
in soil, or over a rotten log.

The bite, which is the actual complaint Almost every call we get about these ants is really a call about being bitten,
and the mechanism is worth explaining because it is unusual.

Where they actually live, and why not your walls The extension guidance is explicit that these ants **rarely nest in homes**, and
that single sentence resolves most of the anxiety we hear.

Telling them from what actually damages buildings This is where the money is, because the two ants get confused and the
consequences are entirely different.

Aphids, honeydew, and the reason they are on your plants If the complaint is ants streaming up a shrub or a fruit tree, the ants are the
symptom.

They are predators, and that is worth something A thatching ant colony takes an enormous number of other insects. In forestry
literature these ants are treated as beneficial for exactly that reason, and
mound-building *Formica* species are protected in parts of Europe on those
grounds.

When it genuinely warrants action There are real conflicts and we would rather name them than pretend the answer
is always no.

What we would actually do Identification first, from a specimen or a good photograph, because the answer
for thatching ants, carpenter ants and moisture ants are three different jobs.

Around this county Thatching ants are ordinary here without being a common service call, and the
pattern follows the terrain rather than the town.
Living with a mound For anybody who would rather keep it, which is a reasonable position:

What we will not sell you We will not treat a thatching ant mound that is not in anybody's way. It is a
predatory colony doing useful work, and killing one to produce an invoice is not
something we are prepared to do.

Hitting a mound with machinery The situation that turns a harmless colony into an afternoon nobody enjoys is
mechanical, and it is the same story we tell about ground-nesting wasps for a
different reason.
Mounds on farm ground and open acreage On rural property the calculation is different again, and usually easier.

What a mound tells you about the ground One last thing worth taking from a thatching ant mound, since it is on your
property whether or not you do anything about it.

title: Thief Ants: The Smallest Ant in the House
sections:
The ant people are not sure is an ant A great many thief ant calls start the same way. Somebody has noticed
something moving on a counter, or a fine line of specks along the edge of a
worktop, and they are not certain whether they are looking at insects or at
dirt.
Recognizing them **Size.** 1.3 to 1.8 mm, monomorphic — every worker the same.

The name, and what it tells you Thief ants earn the name literally. They nest beside other ant colonies, tunnel
into them, and take food and brood.
What they eat Highly predaceous, and then omnivorous on top of that.

Where they nest Outdoors: exposed soil, under stones, boards, and other objects, and in rotting
wood.
Why the identification decides the treatment This is the practical heart of the page.

The chickens question One genuinely specific note, and it is the reason this species gets a mention in
agricultural contexts rather than only domestic ones.

Around this county Thief ants are common and under-reported here, largely because of the size. We
suspect a fair number of "tiny ants in the kitchen" calls that get resolved by
somebody cleaning a cupboard were this species.

What we would actually do **Identify first**, from a specimen. The whole point of this page is that the
answer to "which tiny ant" changes the plan.
What is worth doing yourself More than with most ants, because the scale is domestic.

What we will not sell you We will not name an ant this small without looking at one properly. The
description "tiny yellowish ants in the kitchen" fits at least three species with
different answers, and guessing is not identification.

Why they are hard to exclude Most of this site argues for exclusion. Seal the gap, end the route, and the
problem does not repeat. With thief ants that argument has a limit and it is
honest to state it.

What a trail is telling you With an ant this small the trail is the main evidence available, and it repays
attention before anybody treats.

Outdoors, and the ones that never come in Most thief ants in this county never enter a building at all, and it is worth
saying so because the species is common in soil across the whole area.

The confusion that runs the other way Most of this page is about not mistaking a thief ant for a pharaoh ant. The
reverse mistake happens too, and it is worth a note because the cost falls on
the customer rather than on the outcome.

What we would tell a neighbor Small yellowish ants in the kitchen, no smell when crushed, trail leading to
something greasy: probably this, probably fixable, and worth trying the simple
things for a fortnight before anybody is called.

Why this ant is under-reported We suspect thief ants account for a good many kitchen ant complaints that never
reach a pest control company at all, and the reason is the size.
What we charge for, and what we do not Identification is free, and on this species it is the whole first step.

title: Velvety Tree Ant — Liometopum occidentale
sections:
The ant nobody names correctly There is a good chance that if you have this insect, somebody has already told
you that you have carpenter ants.
The three-part body Start with color, because this is the one feature that settles it across a room.

The velvet in the name The abdomen is covered in very fine hairs, which Utah State names directly and
which the Pacific Northwest handbook describes as a glistening abdomen composed
of dense, fine hair.
The smell This is the fast confirmation and it takes ten seconds.
The four checks that separate it from a carpenter ant Any one of these is usually enough. Together they are conclusive.
Where it lives outdoors The species is named for trees and it means it.

How it gets into a building, and where it goes Utah State describes indoor nests as temporary sites built for foraging, sited
in wall voids and areas with high moisture such as water leaks, and also under
loose bark and rocks and in or under insulation.
Many queens, many nests Here is the structural fact that decides how much work a job is.

The trail is better evidence than the frass With carpenter ants, the heap of coarse shavings below a gallery opening is the
find that organizes the whole job. With this species that evidence is thinner,
because the ants remove less material, and a household waiting to see a frass
pile before taking the problem seriously can wait a long time.

They defend the nest, and it hurts Utah State's description is unusually blunt for an extension publication: the
species is aggressive, inflicts a painful bite, and sprays secretions onto
intruders when disturbed.
Whatcom County, specifically This is a western species and this county gives it a great deal to work with.

Which Liometopum you actually have Worth saying, because the honest answer is that it is sometimes not settled in
the field.

Why the verdict on this page is "treat" Three reasons, and they are the same reasons carpenter ants get the same
verdict.

What competent work involves **Identify properly, and under magnification if the specimen is ambiguous.**
This is the whole reason the page exists. The response for this species overlaps
with the carpenter ant response and diverges from the odorous house ant response
almost completely.

Telling it from the other two it gets confused with **Carpenter ants** are covered above. The color banding and the smell settle it
in under a minute, and the state of the excavation confirms it. The reason to
care is that the two do not get the same treatment plan and a carpenter ant
program aimed at a Liometopum network with several outdoor nest sites will
